sections.h: 0. Principles — every intentional tort starts here
items: Volitional act: the defendant must be in physical control of his actions.
Intent: purpose — a conscious purpose of causing the contact or apprehension — OR knowledge of a substantial certainty that the contact or apprehension will occur (Garratt).

A child might be capable of intent depending on age (Garratt). An insane person is generally capable of intent depending on the nature of the illness, if capable of intending to commit the act in question (McGuire). Mistake as to target does not negate intent (Ransom). Voluntary intoxication does not negate intent. Intent may be transferred to another person or to another cause of action (Talmage).

BATTERY: volitional act → intended to cause → contact → the contact intended must be harmful or offensive to a person of ordinary sensibilities → with the person of the plaintiff or of another, including things attached to him such as clothing or items held or worn (Fisher, extended person rule) → and which causes harmful or offensive contact. Only intent to cause contact is required, not intent to harm or offend. The defendant is responsible for all harm caused, even if unforeseeable — true of all the intentional torts. Complete upon contact.

ASSAULT: volitional act → intended to cause → apprehension of contact → the contact apprehended must be anticipated to be harmful or offensive to a person of ordinary sensibilities → with the person of the plaintiff or of another → and which causes apprehension. Apprehension is best understood as expectation; the contact must be imminent; the defendant must have apparent ability to cause it, a jury question (Western Union); fear is not required but may increase damages. Complete upon apprehension.

FALSE IMPRISONMENT: volitional act → intended to cause, or knowledge of substantial certainty of, confinement → to cause the plaintiff to be restricted or confined to a bounded area → and which causes that confinement → with harm or awareness. Physical restraint is not necessary: abuse of authority, or a threat of harm to the plaintiff, his property, or another person may be enough. There must be no apparent escape, or a risk of harm in escaping. Complete upon confinement with harm or awareness.

IIED: volitional act or series of acts → intentional or reckless → extreme and outrageous → causation → severe emotional distress. Outrageous means conduct so outrageous in character, so extreme in degree, as to go beyond all possible bounds of decency, and to be regarded as atrocious and utterly intolerable in a civilized society (Harris). Character and vulnerability of the victim are factors (Harris). Threats of future violence might suffice (Siliznoff); harm to a family member in the plaintiff's presence might suffice (Taylor). Severe means a severely disabling emotional response; a pre-existing condition must be exacerbated by an increment that itself qualifies as severe (Harris).

TRESPASS TO LAND: volitional act → causes → intrusion onto real property by person or tangible substance, a physical invasion → that interferes with the right to exclusive possession. Not vibration (strict liability or nuisance); not odor, light, or noise (nuisance). The interference is the injury, so separate damages need not be proved. Complete upon entry.

TRESPASS TO CHATTELS: volitional act → causes → interference with the right of exclusive possession by dispossession, damage, or impairment of use → the interference constituting harm to the interest in the chattel. Damages: cost of repair, fair rental value, and losses caused by impairment of use.

CONVERSION: volitional act → causes → interference with the right to exclusive possession by permanent or very long term dispossession or impairment of use, or substantial destruction → such as would warrant payment of the full value of the chattel to the rightful possessor. Incidental losses also recoverable. Seriousness is measured by the § 222A(2) factors: extent and duration of dominion; intent to assert an inconsistent right; good faith; extent and duration of the resulting interference; harm done to the chattel; inconvenience and expense to the other.

sections.h: 2. Affirmative defenses — pleaded and proved by the defendant
items: If both the prima facie case and the affirmative defense are established, the defense defeats the prima facie case. FRCP 8 and similar state rules; may be the subject of dispositive motions.

CONSENT: must be the act of a rational, competent person — intoxication, insanity, and minority may invalidate. Scope may not be exceeded (Mohr; Hackbart). Invalid if obtained by deceit, misrepresentation, or silence where there is a duty to disclose. Consent to illegal acts may or may not be a defense, state by state. Limited to contact within the customs of the sport or activity, which may go beyond the rules of the game (Hackbart). Good faith and a good result will not lead a court to imply consent (Mohr). Three forms: express, apparent (O'Brien), implied (Hackbart).

Medical treatment requires consent, except in emergencies where: the patient is unable to consent because unconscious, incompetent, seriously intoxicated, or mentally ill; the condition imposes a risk of serious harm if treatment is delayed; a reasonable person would consent; and the provider has no reason to believe this particular patient would refuse.

SELF-DEFENSE: anyone may use reasonable force against a threat of battery. No privilege to retaliate. The privilege exists where the defendant reasonably believes force is necessary, even if mistaken. Insults, no matter how vile, create no privilege. No need to wait for the battery. Only necessary force is privileged. Retreat is not required in one's home; at common law it was required elsewhere, but a majority of states now do not require it. Doubts are resolved in favor of the defendant.

DEFENSE OF OTHERS: one may defend another in circumstances in which that person would be privileged to defend himself. The privilege is derivative, and the intervenor is governed by all the same rules. On mistake, courts are divided.

DEFENSE OF PROPERTY: reasonable force may be used to prevent a tort against one's property, but deadly force may not (Katko), and one may not use a mechanical device or dog to do what one could not do oneself (Katko). No privilege where the intrusion is lawful — a meter reader or postal carrier. Unlawful entry into an occupied home is a threat to the occupiers, conceptually different and governed by the Castle Doctrine.

RECOVERY OF PROPERTY (§ 77): the rightful possessor may use non-deadly force to recapture a chattel after a demand for return is ignored, or if he reasonably believes a demand would be useless, or that substantial harm could be done to the chattel before demand can be made — and only if he reasonably believes the chattel can be recovered only by such force.

SHOPKEEPER'S PRIVILEGE (Bonkowski): a retail merchant may, upon reasonable suspicion that a customer has taken goods, use reasonable force — never deadly — to detain the customer on the premises for a reasonable time to investigate. Reasonableness is for the court in the first instance, then the jury.

PUBLIC NECESSITY (Surocco): a defense to all the intentional torts studied. Property may be destroyed, or otherwise tortious conduct committed, when necessary or apparently necessary to prevent great harm to the community. No compensation at common law, though many states now provide it by statute. Includes quarantine and other restraints that would otherwise be false imprisonment or battery. Private property rights are subordinate to the safety of society.

PRIVATE NECESSITY (Lake Erie Transport): an incomplete defense. Private property may be used or taken to avoid a greater harm to person or other property. No legal wrong is committed, so the owner may not compel the user to desist — but the user must pay the value of any damage, without punitive damages. If the owner forces the user to desist and harm results, the owner is liable.
AUTHORITY OF LAW AND DISCIPLINE: now largely statutory, with many changes especially as to the parental privilege to discipline.

JUSTIFICATION: a catch-all under Rest. 2d § 10 — a privilege to commit an otherwise tortious act may arise in circumstances unanticipated before. The test in Sindle is a measure of necessity, the concept rather than the defense, under those particular circumstances. The categories of privilege are not carved in stone.

CONTAMINATED FOOD: the defendant was engaged in the business of manufacturing or selling the food product → the food product was contaminated, meaning poison, putrefaction, or foreign objects, but not bones and stones natural to the food → the product reached the consumer in substantially the same condition as when it left the defendant's control → the contamination was a cause → of the injury suffered by the plaintiff.

WILD ANIMALS: the defendant owned, kept, or harbored a wild animal, and must have been the last to have kept or harbored it → the type of animal has dangerous or vicious propensities arising from its wildness, as to which scienter is PRESUMED → the animal, as a result of its wildness, caused → harm to the plaintiff's person or property. If the harm came from some other characteristic, strict liability will not lie, though negligence might.

UNUSUALLY DANGEROUS DOMESTIC ANIMALS: the defendant kept, possessed, or harbored — ownership not required → an abnormally dangerous domestic animal, dangerousness usually arising from other attacks or behavior creating a risk of harm → scienter: actual or constructive knowledge of the abnormal dangerousness, NOT presumed as with wild animals → the animal, as a result of its abnormal dangerousness, caused → harm to the plaintiff's person or property.

ULTRAHAZARDOUS ACTIVITIES: the defendant undertook an activity → the activity is ultrahazardous → one or more of the risks that make it ultrahazardous → caused → harm to the plaintiff. For blasting those risks are concussion of air, vibration of ground, and flying debris.

§ 519: one who carries on an abnormally dangerous activity is subject to liability for harm to the person, land or chattels of another resulting from the activity, although he has exercised the utmost care to prevent the harm. This strict liability is limited to the kind of harm the possibility of which makes the activity abnormally dangerous.

§ 520 FACTORS — not elements: (a) existence of a high degree of risk of some harm; (b) likelihood that the resulting harm will be great, likelihood not meaning probability; (c) inability to eliminate the risk by the exercise of reasonable care; (d) extent to which the activity is not a matter of common usage; (e) inappropriateness of the activity to the place where it is carried on — (d) and (e) generally read together; and (f) extent to which its value to the community is outweighed by its dangerous attributes.
DEFENSE: voluntary assumption of a known risk. At common law, and for this class, the only defense you need to know.

sections.h: 4. Negligence — duty, breach, causation in fact, proximate causation, damages
items: DUTY is a legal obligation to act as an ordinary, reasonable, prudent person under all circumstances. Its content comes from common sense, custom of an industry or trade, standards of a profession, statute, ordinance, or regulation, or case law.

THE REASONABLE PERSON: everyone is presumed to be one. Physical limitations are accounted for — a reasonable wheelchair-bound, blind, or deaf person. Mental ones generally are not: low IQ, insanity, and lack of knowledge all get the ordinary reasonable person. Superior knowledge must be used. For children, it depends.

CHILDREN AS DEFENDANTS: held to the standard of a child of like age, education, intelligence and experience — an objective standard based on children with similar characteristics, not on this particular child. When conducting dangerous activities generally reserved for adults, an adult standard applies; there is no clear rule, so look at the thing the child is using. A gun is always the adult standard.

CUSTOM is evidence of the content of a duty an industry imposes on itself. It does not bind court or jury but is important evidence, and courts ordinarily follow it — subject to challenge on Hand Formula considerations (Helling v. Carey).

NEGLIGENCE PER SE applies where a statute, regulation, or ordinance is intended to protect a class of persons including the plaintiff AND from injury of the type suffered. Both are required; if either fails, treat the case as common law negligence, though the statute may still supply ideas for the content of duty. Where it applies the court borrows the duty, and it binds the jury on duty and breach unless obedience is excused. Excuse may be built into the statute or adopted from § 288A: incapacity; neither knowing nor having reason to know of the occasion for compliance; inability to comply after reasonable diligence; an emergency not due to the actor's own misconduct; or compliance involving a greater risk of harm — the last being the most important. The violation must still be a cause in fact and a proximate cause, though proximate cause is rarely at issue because the plaintiff is by nature a foreseeable plaintiff suffering foreseeable harm.

PROFESSIONAL STANDARD: a professional must possess and exercise the knowledge and skill of an ordinary member of the profession in good standing; expert testimony is generally necessary. For physicians the standard is national — the locality rule is out — and the duty includes informed consent.

INFORMED CONSENT: the physician must inform the patient, before consent is given, that an adverse outcome is a risk even if the treatment is properly performed. Materiality is measured by what would be material to a reasonable patient in the same situation. Failure to inform is handled as negligence, not battery.

DUTY FROM ANOTHER'S FORESEEABLE NEGLIGENCE: the foreseeable negligence of one tortfeasor can create a duty in another — barriers at a roadside job site (Derdiarian), lighting in a parking lot, a landlord's security. The extent of the duty depends on the risk.

WHEN THERE IS NO OBVIOUS SOURCE: reverse engineer. Review the sequence from the defendant's conduct to the harm, determine what he could have done differently to prevent it, and treat that conduct as the possible duty. Its cost becomes the cost of avoidance under Hand.

LEARNED HAND'S FORMULA: standing at the place and time just before the conduct and looking forward, weigh the likelihood that some harm would occur and the likely severity of that harm — together, the RISK — against the cost of avoiding it, including the cost to this defendant, to others similarly situated, and social costs. This is social policy, not math; it compares incommensurables. It is both inefficient and unfair to impose a cost of avoidance too high for the risk, so even with real risk and measurable cost there might still be no duty.

No compensation is required at common law. The rationale in destruction of property cases may have been that this particular property would have been destroyed anyway. Many states have provided for compensation by statute.

The principle includes quarantine and other physical restraints that would otherwise be false imprisonment or battery. Private property rights are subordinate to the safety of society and the community.

components: An INCOMPLETE defense to trespass to real property and the other intentional torts
Private property may be used or taken to avoid a greater harm to person or other property
No legal wrong is committed, so the owner may not compel the user to desist
The user must still pay the value of any damage to the property
But no punitive damages
If the owner forces the user to desist and harm results, the owner is liable
model: Private necessity is an incomplete defense to trespass to real property and to the other intentional torts (Lake Erie Transport). Private property may be used or taken in order to avoid a greater harm to person or other property.

No legal wrong is committed thereby, and therefore the owner may not compel the user to desist. But the user must still pay the value of any damage to the property, though no punitive damages. If the owner forces the user to desist and harm results to the user or the user's property, the owner is liable.

blurts.topic: Authority of law, discipline, and justification
components: Authority of law and discipline are regulated by statute
Many statutory changes, especially the parental privilege to discipline
Be aware they exist, but they are now largely statutory
Justification is a catch-all under Rest. 2d § 10 [Sindle]
A privilege to commit an otherwise tortious act may arise in circumstances unanticipated before
The test in Sindle is simply a measure of necessity under those particular circumstances
The categories of privilege are not carved in stone; the concept admits of flexibility
model: Authority of law and discipline are regulated by statute, with many statutory changes, especially as to the parental privilege to discipline. Be aware they are out there, but they are now largely based on statute.

Justification is a catch-all concept, subsumed under Restatement (2d) § 10, that a privilege to commit an act or acts otherwise tortious may arise in various circumstances unanticipated before (Sindle). The test in Sindle is simply a measure of necessity — not the defense, the concept — under those particular circumstances. The message is that the categories of privilege are not carved in stone for all time; the concept admits of flexibility.

components: Duty
Breach
Causation in fact
Proximate causation
Damages
model: Prima facie case for negligence: (1) duty; (2) breach; (3) causation in fact; (4) proximate causation; and (5) damages.

components: A legal obligation to act as an ordinary, reasonable, prudent person under all circumstances
That is the GENERAL duty
Sources: common sense, custom of an industry or trade, standards of a profession
Statute, ordinance, or regulation
Case law
model: Duty is a legal obligation to act as an ordinary, reasonable, prudent person under all the circumstances. That is the general duty.
Its content may come from common sense, the custom of an industry or trade, the standards of a profession, a statute, ordinance, or regulation, or case law.

components: Everyone is presumed to be the ordinary, reasonably prudent person
Physical limitations are accounted for — a reasonable wheelchair-bound, blind, or deaf person
Low IQ — ordinary reasonable person
Insane — ordinary reasonable person
Lacking knowledge — ordinary reasonable person
Superior knowledge — must use that knowledge
Child — it depends
model: In reality everyone is presumed to be the ordinary, reasonably prudent person, with caveats.
Physical limitations are accounted for: the duty is that of a reasonable wheelchair-bound person, or a reasonable blind or deaf person, to others.

Mental abilities and development are not, with one exception. Low IQ: ordinary reasonable person. Insane: ordinary reasonable person. Lacking knowledge: ordinary reasonable person. Superior knowledge: must use that knowledge. Child: it depends.

components: Held to the standard of care of a child of like age, education, intelligence and experience
This is an OBJECTIVE standard
Based on children with characteristics similar to this child, not on this particular child
When conducting dangerous activities generally reserved for adults, children are held to an adult standard
No clear rule — look at the thing the child is using
A gun is ALWAYS the adult standard
model: Children as defendants are held to the standard of care of a child of like age, education, intelligence and experience. This is an objective standard, meaning it is a general standard based on children with characteristics similar to those of this child, but it is not based on this particular child.

When conducting dangerous activities generally reserved for adults, children are held to an adult standard. There is no clear rule for which activities qualify; look at the thing the child is using — compare a tractor, snowmobile, or gun with small toys, a ball, or a bicycle. A gun is always the adult standard.

components: Common sense, common or local knowledge
Custom of industry or trade; standards of an industry
Custom is evidence of the content of a duty the industry imposes on itself
It does not bind court or jury but is important evidence — courts ordinarily follow it
May be challenged on the basis of Hand Formula considerations [Helling v. Carey]
Case law — an earlier case imposing or declining a duty might bind us, depending on its value as precedent
model: Sources of duty: common sense, and common or local knowledge.

Custom of an industry or trade, and the standards of an industry. This is evidence of the content of a duty that a particular industry, trade, or profession imposes on itself. It does not bind the court or jury but is important evidence, and courts ordinarily follow it. It may be challenged on the basis of Hand Formula considerations (Helling v. Carey).
Case law: if an earlier case has imposed or declined to impose a duty, that case might bind us in future cases, depending on its value as precedent.

components: The statute, regulation, or ordinance must be intended to protect a class of persons INCLUDING the plaintiff
…from injury of the TYPE suffered by the plaintiff
BOTH must be met or negligence per se cannot be applied
If not met, treat the cause of action as common law negligence
The court 'borrows' the duty of conduct from these sources as the negligence duty
Binds the jury on duty and breach, unless obedience to the statute is excused
The violation must also be a cause in fact of the harm
And a proximate cause — rarely an issue, because the plaintiff is a foreseeable plaintiff suffering foreseeable harm
model: Negligence per se applies when a statute, regulation, or ordinance is intended (a) to protect a class of persons including the plaintiff, and (b) from injury of the type suffered by the plaintiff. Both requirements must be met or negligence per se cannot be applied.

In such a case, treat the cause of action as common law negligence. The statute might still be useful as a source of ideas for the content of duty, but need not be adopted per se by the court, and breach, cause in fact, and proximate cause are applied as they would ordinarily be.

Where it applies, the court borrows the duty of conduct from these sources as the negligence duty, and it binds the jury on duty and breach unless obedience to the statute is excused. Excuse may, but need not, be built into the statute itself, or it may be adopted from the list in Restatement (2d) § 288A. The most important excuse is that obedience to the statute would be more dangerous than disobedience.

The violation must also be a cause in fact of the harm, and a proximate cause — though proximate cause is rarely an issue, because by the nature of negligence per se the plaintiff is a foreseeable plaintiff suffering a foreseeable harm.

components: A professional or person with special skill must possess and exercise the knowledge and skill of an ordinary member of the profession in good standing
Expert testimony is generally necessary
Physician, specialist, attorney, pilot, electrician
For physicians the standard of care is NATIONAL
The old locality rule is out
A physician's duty includes informed consent
model: A person who is a professional or has special skill is required to possess and exercise the knowledge and skill of an ordinary member of the profession or occupation in good standing. Expert testimony is generally necessary.

Examples: physician, specialist such as a neurologist or psychiatrist, attorney, pilot, electrician. For physicians the standard of care is national — the old locality rule is out. A physician's duty includes informed consent.

components: Part of a physician's duty and standard of care
Usually invoked when treatment is properly performed within the standard of care but the patient has an adverse outcome anyway
The duty is to inform, BEFORE the patient consents, that the adverse outcome is a risk even if treatment is properly performed
Based on facts and risks material to the patient's decision
Measured by what would be material to a REASONABLE PATIENT in the same situation
Failure to inform is handled as negligence, not battery
model: Informed consent is part of a physician's duty and standard of care. It is usually invoked in litigation when treatment is properly performed within the standard of care but the patient has an adverse outcome anyway.

The duty of the physician is to inform, before the patient gives consent to the procedure or medication, that the adverse outcome is a risk even if the treatment is properly performed. It is based on facts and risks material to the patient's decision, measured by those facts that would be material to a reasonable patient in the same situation as the plaintiff-patient.
Failure to inform may lead to liability, but is handled as negligence, not battery.

components: Sometimes the foreseeable negligence of one tortfeasor becomes the basis of a duty imposed on another
A general contractor had a duty to put up barriers because negligent driving is foreseeable [Derdiarian]
Duty to have proper lighting in a parking lot where crimes or negligent driving are foreseeable
Duty of a landlord to provide security sufficient for the risk — locks, cameras
Based on foreseeability of intentional torts and crimes in that place
The extent of the duty here depends on the risk
model: Sometimes the foreseeable negligence of one tortfeasor becomes the basis of a duty imposed on another tortfeasor. A general contractor had a duty to put barriers up to protect workers on a roadside job site because negligent driving is foreseeable (Derdiarian).

Other examples: a duty to have proper lighting in a parking lot where crimes or negligent driving — backing out of parking spaces — are foreseeable; and the duty of a landlord to provide security sufficient for the risk, such as locks and cameras, based on the foreseeability of intentional torts and crimes in that place. The extent of the duty here depends on the risk.

blurts.topic: When there is no obvious source of duty
components: Odd or unfamiliar facts require a more elaborate approach
Review the sequence of facts leading from the defendant's conduct to the plaintiff's harm
Determine what the defendant could have done differently to prevent or minimize the harm
Reverse engineer the facts
Whatever conduct would have prevented the harm is the conduct we consider as a possible duty
The cost of that conduct is the cost of avoidance under the Hand Formula
model: Odd or unfamiliar facts require a more elaborate approach. Review the sequence of facts leading from the defendant's conduct to the plaintiff's harm, and determine what the defendant could have done differently that would have prevented or minimized the harm.

Reverse engineer the facts: whatever conduct, to do or to refrain from, that would have prevented the harm, is the conduct we consider as a possible duty. Note that the cost of that conduct is the cost of avoidance that we consider under Learned Hand's formula.

components: Once we decide what conduct would have avoided the harm, we decide whether it ought to be imposed as a legal duty
Put yourself at the place and time just before the conduct took place
Looking forward: the likelihood, as understood then, that SOME harm would occur
The likely severity of that harm should it occur
Those two together are the RISK
Against that, the cost of avoiding the harm by complying with the contemplated duty
Including cost to this defendant, to others similarly situated, and social costs
This is social policy, not math
model: Once we decide what conduct by the defendant would have avoided the harm, we must decide whether it ought to be imposed as a legal duty. To do so we put ourselves metaphorically at the place where, and at the time just before, the conduct took place.

Looking forward, we consider the likelihood, as we would have understood it then, that some harm would occur, and the likely severity of that harm should it occur. Those two together are the RISK. On the other side we evaluate the cost of avoiding that harm and that risk by complying with the duty we contemplate — including the cost to this defendant, the cost to others similarly situated, and the social costs, if any, of imposing the duty. This is social policy, not math.

We then compare the risk to the cost of avoidance. Unavoidably it requires comparing incommensurables; Judge Hand says so himself. It is both inefficient and unfair to impose on defendants a cost of avoidance too high for the risk involved. So even if there is risk and a reasonably measurable cost of avoidance, there might still be no duty.

components: Issue: whether π can establish a prima facie case against Δ for [tort]
A claim is ESTABLISHED, not 'provided'
Affirmative defenses come after the prima facie case, and Δ pleads and proves them
Open the application with 'on these facts' or 'in the instant case'
Take the elements one at a time; link the rule directly to the facts
Δ is SUBJECT TO LIABILITY, not 'guilty'
Intrusion ONTO real property; Δ ENTERED (past tense)
Do not bolt 'no reasonable means of escape' onto the FI rule — that is what confined means
model: Frame the issue as whether the party can establish a prima facie case against the other party for a named cause of action. Do not recite facts in the issue, and do not frame the issue around Δ's affirmative defense — consent and the other privileges are pleaded and proved by Δ after the prima facie case is established.

Open the application with 'on these facts,' 'in the instant case,' or simply 'here.' Take the elements one at a time and link the governing rule directly to the facts that satisfy each; a sweep across 'every element' invites the question which one, and how.

Use the working verbs: π establishes a prima facie case; Δ pleads and proves an affirmative defense; a privilege attaches; Δ is subject to liability. Avoid 'guilty,' which is criminal, and avoid declaring an issue 'cut and dried.'

components: Strike 'clearly,' 'obviously,' 'no question,' 'cut and dried,' 'pretty much'
These assert the conclusion the analysis is supposed to earn
Name the conduct, tie it to the element, state the legal consequence
Do not raise an argument you concede the facts will not support
Either analyze the counterargument or omit it
model: Subjective characterizations do no analytical work. 'Clearly,' 'obviously,' 'there was no question,' 'cut and dried' — each announces a result in place of the reasoning that should produce it. Delete them; if the sentence still stands, they were padding, and if it collapses, the analysis was never there.
Replace them with the move itself: name the conduct, tie it to the element it satisfies, and state the legal consequence.

The same discipline applies to counterarguments. Raising an argument and then conceding the record will not support it spends words without advancing the answer. Either the facts support it, in which case analyze it and explain why it fails, or they do not, in which case leave it out.

cards.scenario: A diner cracks a molar on a fragment of shell in a bowl of clam chowder at a restaurant. She sues in strict liability for contaminated food. Which statement best analyzes the claim?
options: She recovers — any foreign material in food is contamination
She does not recover on this theory — shell in chowder is natural to the food, the 'bones and stones' limitation
She recovers only if the restaurant was negligent in straining the chowder
She recovers because the restaurant is in the business of selling food
cards.explanation: Contamination means poison, putrefaction, or foreign objects. The doctrine is not applied to harm caused by bones and stones natural to the food — shell in a shellfish dish is the paradigm case. A negligence claim might still lie.
cards.why: The 'foreign object' element does real work; natural components are outside it.

cards.scenario: A sealed jar of peanut butter leaves the factory clean. A grocery stocker punctures the seal with a box cutter, and mold develops. The buyer sues the manufacturer in strict liability. What result?
options: The manufacturer is subject to liability — it manufactured the product that injured the buyer
Manufacturer not subject to liability — the product did not reach the consumer in substantially the same condition as when it left the manufacturer's control
The manufacturer is subject to liability because mold is putrefaction
The manufacturer is subject to liability unless it proves the stocker acted intentionally
cards.explanation: The third element requires the product to reach the consumer in substantially the same condition as when it left the defendant's control. An intervening puncture breaks that chain as to the manufacturer, whatever the grocery's own exposure may be.
cards.why: Element three is where post-sale tampering and mishandling get resolved.

cards.scenario: A neighbor bakes a pie as a gift. It contains a shard of glass from a broken mixing bowl, and the recipient is injured. Can π establish a prima facie case in strict liability for contaminated food?
options: Yes — glass is a foreign object and it caused injury
No — the neighbor was not engaged in the business of manufacturing or selling the food product
Yes — the pie reached the recipient in the same condition
No — gifts can never give rise to tort liability
cards.explanation: The first element requires that the defendant be engaged in the business of manufacturing or selling the food at issue. A casual gift-giver is not, so strict liability does not lie — though negligence might.
cards.why: Element one screens out the non-commercial defendant before you ever reach contamination.

cards.scenario: A canner proves it uses the most advanced sterilization equipment available and inspects every lot, yet one can of soup left the plant carrying botulinum toxin and poisons a consumer. Is Δ subject to liability?
options: No — reasonable care, indeed the utmost care, is a complete answer
Yes — strict liability is liability without fault; the care exercised is irrelevant to the prima facie case
No — unless the consumer proves a specific defect in the process
Yes — but only for medical expenses, not pain and suffering
cards.explanation: Strict liability is liability without fault. Once the elements are made out, the defendant's care — even the utmost care — does not defeat the claim. That is precisely what distinguishes it from negligence.
cards.why: TRICKY: the facts invite a reasonable-care answer that has no place in a strict liability prima facie case.

cards.scenario: A consumer bites into a burger and finds a small metal screw, which he spits out unharmed. He is disgusted but suffers no physical injury and no illness. Can π establish a prima facie case in strict liability against Δ?
options: Yes — the presence of a foreign object completes the tort
No — the prima facie case requires that the contamination cause an injury suffered by the plaintiff, and none occurred
Yes — disgust is an injury for strict liability purposes
No — screws are not foreign objects within the meaning of the rule
cards.explanation: The last two elements are causation and injury suffered by the plaintiff. A foreign object found but causing no injury leaves the prima facie case incomplete. Contrast battery, which is complete on contact without proof of damage.
cards.why: TRICKY: strict liability requires actual harm — unlike the intentional torts, there is no nominal-damages version.

cards.scenario: A private collector keeps a tiger in a reinforced enclosure. It escapes through a gate a vandal cuts open and mauls a passerby. The collector proves he took every conceivable precaution. Is Δ subject to liability?
options: No — his precautions establish reasonable care
Yes — scienter is presumed for wild animals and liability attaches without fault
No — the vandal's act breaks the chain
Yes — but only if the collector knew this tiger had bitten before
cards.explanation: For wild animals the defendant is held to knowledge of the dangers arising from the animal's wildness; scienter is presumed. Liability is without fault, so precautions do not answer the prima facie case.
cards.why: Presumed scienter is the whole point of the wild-animal category.

cards.scenario: A zoo's elephant, startled by thunder, sits down on a visitor's foot while being led to its enclosure. The visitor sues in strict liability. Which statement best analyzes the claim?
options: Strict liability applies — an elephant is a wild animal and it caused harm
Strict liability likely does not apply — the harm flowed from the animal's size and clumsiness, not from a dangerous propensity arising from its wildness
Strict liability applies because scienter is presumed
Strict liability applies unless the zoo proves the thunder was unforeseeable
cards.explanation: The caveat: if the harm was caused by some characteristic of the animal other than its wildness, strict liability will not lie, though negligence might. Crushing weight is not a vicious propensity arising from wildness.
cards.why: TRICKY: 'wild animal' plus 'harm' is not enough — the harm must flow from the wildness.

cards.scenario: A trapper sells a captured wolf to a roadside attraction, which keeps it for a year before it bites a customer. The customer sues the trapper. What result?
options: The trapper is subject to liability — he originally captured and harbored the wolf
Trapper not subject to liability — the defendant must have been the last to have kept or harbored the animal
The trapper is subject to liability jointly with the attraction
The trapper is subject to liability because scienter is presumed as to wolves
cards.explanation: The element is that the defendant owned, kept, or harbored the animal, and the defendant must have been the last to have kept or harbored it. Having passed the wolf on a year earlier, the trapper is outside the rule.
cards.why: The 'last to keep or harbor' gloss decides who among a chain of possessors answers.

cards.scenario: A homeowner discovers a colony of bats living in his attic and does nothing about them for months. A guest is bitten. Is the homeowner within the wild animal rule?
options: No — he never acquired or purchased the bats
Potentially yes — the element is satisfied by one who owned, KEPT, or HARBORED the animal, and harboring can be established by knowingly permitting an animal to remain
No — bats are not wild animals
Yes — but only if he fed them
cards.explanation: The element reaches one who owned, kept, or harbored the animal. Harboring is broader than ownership, so knowingly allowing wild animals to remain on the premises can satisfy it.
cards.why: TRICKY: ownership is only one of three ways in; harboring requires no title at all.

cards.scenario: A rattlesnake kept as a pet escapes and a neighbor, seeing it, leaps backward off a porch and breaks an ankle. The snake never touched her. Which statement best analyzes the claim?
options: π cannot establish a prima facie case — the animal must physically contact the plaintiff
The claim turns on whether harm resulted from a dangerous propensity arising from wildness; a flight reaction to a venomous snake is closely tied to that propensity
π cannot establish a prima facie case — fright is not harm to person or property
Strict liability is automatic once the snake escapes
cards.explanation: The elements require that the animal, as a result of its wildness, caused harm to the plaintiff's person or property. Nothing requires contact; what matters is whether the harm flowed from the propensity arising from the animal's wildness.
cards.why: Causation here is about the source of the harm, not the mechanism of touching.

cards.scenario: A dog with no history of aggression bites a mail carrier for the first time. The owner had no reason to think it dangerous. Can π establish a prima facie case in strict liability against Δ?
options: Yes — dog owners are strictly liable at common law
No — scienter is not presumed for domestic animals, and the owner had neither actual nor constructive knowledge of abnormal dangerousness
Yes — biting is inherently abnormally dangerous behavior
No — mail carriers assume the risk
cards.explanation: Unlike wild animals, scienter is not presumed for domestic animals. The plaintiff must show actual or constructive knowledge of the abnormal dangerousness, which typically arises from prior attacks or risk-creating behavior. A first bite by a placid dog fails that element.
cards.why: This is the whole distinction between the two animal categories.

cards.scenario: A dog has lunged and snapped at three delivery drivers over six months, each time restrained just in time. It has never made contact. It then bites a neighbor. What is the owner's strongest argument?
options: No scienter — the dog had never actually bitten anyone before
The argument fails: abnormal dangerousness usually arises from other attacks OR other behavior creating a risk of harm, and repeated lunging supplies constructive knowledge
The neighbor assumed the risk by approaching
Domestic animals can never support strict liability
cards.explanation: The outline defines abnormal dangerousness as usually arising from other attacks on people or animals, or other behavior that creates a risk of harm. Prior contact is not required — behavior creating risk suffices, and it supplies at least constructive knowledge.
cards.why: TRICKY: the 'every dog gets one free bite' intuition overreads the rule; risk-creating behavior counts.

cards.scenario: A man agrees to watch his brother's dog for a week. He knows the dog has bitten two people. It bites a visitor on day three. He argues he does not own the dog. What result?
options: Not subject to liability — the element requires ownership
Subject to liability — the element is satisfied by one who kept, possessed, or harbored the animal; ownership is not required
Not subject to liability — scienter belongs to the brother
Subject to liability only if he was negligent in restraining it
cards.explanation: The first element is that the defendant kept, possessed, or harbored the animal, and expressly need not own it. He knew of the prior bites, so scienter is satisfied as to him.
cards.why: Possession plus knowledge is enough; title is beside the point.

cards.scenario: A horse known to kick anyone who approaches from behind instead spooks at a siren and tramples a bystander in front of it. Can π establish a prima facie case in strict liability against Δ?
options: Yes — the owner knew the horse was abnormally dangerous
Likely no — the harm must result from the abnormal dangerousness the defendant knew about, and trampling while spooked is a different characteristic
Yes — scienter as to any dangerous trait suffices for all harms
No — horses are never abnormally dangerous domestic animals
cards.explanation: The caveat applies: if the harm was caused by some characteristic other than the dangerousness in question, strict liability does not lie. The known propensity was kicking from behind; a spooked trampling is a different characteristic. Negligence might still lie.
cards.why: TRICKY: scienter must match the propensity that actually caused the harm.

cards.scenario: How does the scienter requirement for wild animals differ from that for abnormally dangerous domestic animals?
options: Both are presumed
For wild animals scienter is presumed; for domestic animals the plaintiff must show actual or constructive knowledge
Both require proof of actual knowledge
For wild animals it must be proved; for domestic animals it is presumed
cards.explanation: Wild animals: the defendant is held to knowledge of the dangers arising from the animal's wildness — scienter is presumed. Domestic animals: scienter is not presumed and must be established as actual or constructive knowledge of the abnormal dangerousness.
cards.why: The single most testable contrast between the two animal categories.

cards.text: One who carries on an {{abnormally}} {{dangerous}} activity is subject to liability for harm to the person, land or chattels of another resulting from the activity, although he has exercised the {{utmost}} {{care}} to prevent the harm. This strict liability is limited to the kind of {{harm}}, the possibility of which makes the activity abnormally dangerous.
cards.why: The second sentence is the scope limitation — it is why harm falling outside the characteristic risk is not covered.

cards.prompt: Name the six § 520 factors for determining whether an activity is abnormally dangerous.
answer: (a) Existence of a high degree of risk of some harm to the person, land or chattels of others;
(b) Likelihood that the harm that results from it will be great — likelihood does not mean probability;
(c) Inability to eliminate the risk by the exercise of reasonable care — the defendant can be liable even if not negligent;
(d) Extent to which the activity is not a matter of common usage;
(e) Inappropriateness of the activity to the place where it is carried on; and
(f) Extent to which its value to the community is outweighed by its dangerous attributes.
These are FACTORS, not elements of a cause of action.
cards.fallback: High degree of {{risk}}; likelihood the harm will be {{great}}; inability to eliminate the risk by {{reasonable}} care; extent to which the activity is not a matter of {{common}} usage; {{inappropriateness}} to the place; and the extent to which its {{value}} to the community is outweighed by its dangerous attributes.
cards.why: Factors (d) and (e) are generally read together.

cards.scenario: A blasting contractor sets off a charge. A mile away, a farmer's mink, alarmed by the noise, kill their own kits. The farmer sues in strict liability. Which statement best analyzes the claim?
options: Recovery — blasting is ultrahazardous and the harm resulted from it

No recovery on this theory — § 519 limits strict liability to the kind of harm the possibility of which makes the activity abnormally dangerous, and nervous mink are outside the characteristic risks of concussion, vibration, and flying debris
Recovery — § 520 factors all favor the farmer
No recovery — mink are not property
cards.explanation: Section 519's second sentence limits strict liability to the kind of harm the possibility of which makes the activity abnormally dangerous. For blasting those risks are concussion of air, vibration of ground, and flying debris — not the reaction of nervous animals at a distance.
cards.why: TRICKY: the scope limitation in § 519 is the trap; causation alone is not enough.

cards.scenario: A defendant argues that its activity cannot be abnormally dangerous because it satisfies only four of the six § 520 factors. What is the strongest response?
options: Correct — a majority of the factors must be satisfied
Incorrect — these are factors to be considered, not elements of a cause of action; no fixed number must be met
Correct — all six must be satisfied
Incorrect — only factor (a) matters
cards.explanation: Section 520 says the listed considerations are factors to be weighed in determining whether an activity is abnormally dangerous. The outline flags this explicitly: they are not elements of a cause of action.
cards.why: Factors versus elements is a distinction the professor called out on the page.

cards.scenario: Under § 520(b), the likelihood that the harm resulting will be great. What does 'likelihood' mean here?
options: The statistical probability that harm will occur
Not probability — the factor asks about the magnitude of the harm if it does occur
The chance the defendant will be sued
The frequency with which the activity is conducted
cards.explanation: The outline flags this specifically: likelihood does not mean probability. Factor (a) already addresses the degree of risk; factor (b) is about how great the harm will be should it materialize.
cards.why: TRICKY: the ordinary meaning of 'likelihood' points the wrong way here.

cards.scenario: A company stores large quantities of explosives in a dense residential neighborhood. Which § 520 factors do this location facts speak to most directly?
options: (a) and (b), risk and gravity
(d) and (e), the extent to which the activity is not a matter of common usage and its inappropriateness to the place where it is carried on — generally read together
(c) alone, inability to eliminate the risk
(f) alone, value to the community
cards.explanation: Factors (d) and (e) — not a matter of common usage, and inappropriateness to the place — are generally read together, and location facts drive both.
cards.why: The outline notes that 4 and 5 are read as a pair.

cards.scenario: A blasting company proves it followed every industry safety protocol and the shot was executed perfectly. Debris still damages a home. What is the legal effect of that showing on the prima facie case?
options: It defeats liability — reasonable care is a defense

None on the prima facie case — § 519 imposes liability although the actor exercised the utmost care, and § 520(c) treats inability to eliminate risk by reasonable care as a factor pointing toward strict liability
It reduces damages proportionally
It shifts the burden to the plaintiff to prove negligence
cards.explanation: Section 519 states liability attaches although the actor has exercised the utmost care. Indeed § 520(c) — inability to eliminate the risk by the exercise of reasonable care — is one reason the activity is treated as abnormally dangerous in the first place.
cards.why: Care is not merely irrelevant; its insufficiency is part of the justification.

cards.scenario: A visitor to a private zoo climbs over a warning barrier to photograph a bear and is clawed. The zoo raises a defense to strict liability. On which affirmative defense should the zoo rely?
options: Contributory negligence
Voluntary assumption of a known risk
Comparative fault
Consent to the animal's wildness
cards.explanation: At common law, and for this course, voluntary assumption of a known risk is the only defense to strict liability you need to know. Deliberately crossing a barrier to approach a bear is the paradigm.
cards.why: One defense, cleanly stated — do not import negligence defenses.

cards.scenario: A homeowner is inattentive and fails to notice blasting warning signs before walking near a construction site, where flying debris injures him. The contractor pleads contributory negligence. What result under the common law rule applied in this course?
options: Complete bar — contributory negligence bars any tort claim
Not the operative defense — the only defense to know here is voluntary assumption of a KNOWN risk, and mere inattention is not knowing acceptance
Damages reduced by his percentage of fault
Complete bar because he was on the premises voluntarily
cards.explanation: The defense is voluntary assumption of a known risk. Carelessness that falls short of knowingly accepting the risk does not fit it, and ordinary contributory negligence is not the defense identified for strict liability in this course.
cards.why: TRICKY: 'voluntary' and 'known' are both doing work — inattention satisfies neither.

cards.scenario: A man having an epileptic seizure strikes a bystander with his flailing arm. Can π establish a prima facie case for battery against Δ?
options: Yes — the contact was harmful and he caused it
No — there is no volitional act; he was not in physical control of his actions
Yes — under transferred intent
No — but only because he lacked purpose to strike
cards.explanation: Every intentional tort begins with a volitional act, meaning the defendant was in physical control of his actions. A seizure is not volitional, so the analysis ends before intent is reached.
cards.why: Volitional act is a separate, prior element — do not collapse it into intent.

cards.scenario: A shooter aims at what he believes is a stray dog worrying his sheep. It is in fact his neighbor's prize show dog. He argues mistake. What result?
options: No intent — he did not intend to shoot that dog
Intent established — mistake as to target does not negate intent [Ransom]
No intent — his purpose was to protect livestock
Intent only if he was negligent in identifying the animal
cards.explanation: Mistake as to target does not negate intent (Ransom). He intended the act and its consequence; that he was mistaken about which animal he was shooting is immaterial.
cards.why: Mistake and lack of intent are different things — mistake goes to identity, not volition or purpose.

cards.scenario: A defendant drinks heavily, then deliberately shoves a stranger at a bar. He argues intoxication negated intent. What result?
options: No intent — intoxication negates the mental state
Intent established — voluntary intoxication does not negate intent
No intent unless he remembers the shove
Intent only if he was a habitual drinker
cards.explanation: Voluntary intoxication does not negate intent. The rule is stated flatly in the outline; the shove was volitional and purposeful.
cards.why: Contrast the criminal law's specific-intent treatment, which does not carry over here.

cards.scenario: A defendant with a serious mental illness believes his neighbor is an intruder and strikes him. Under McGuire, may Δ form the requisite intent?
options: No — insanity is a complete defense to intentional torts
Generally yes — an insane person is capable of intent depending on the nature of the illness, if that person is capable of intending to commit the act in question
No — unless he was adjudicated competent
Yes — insanity is never relevant to any element
cards.explanation: Under McGuire, an insane person is generally capable of intent depending on the nature of the illness, if that person is capable of intending to commit the act in question. The delusional motive does not defeat intent to strike.
cards.why: Note the qualifier: it depends on the nature of the illness and capacity to intend the act.

cards.scenario: A five-year-old pulls a chair away as an adult begins to sit, having no wish to hurt her but understanding she will land on the floor. Under Garratt, is the intent element satisfied?
options: No — a five-year-old is legally incapable of intent
Yes — knowledge of a substantial certainty that the contact will occur satisfies intent, and a child might be capable of intent depending on age
No — he lacked the purpose to cause harm
Yes — but only under transferred intent
cards.explanation: Intent is satisfied by purpose OR by knowledge of a substantial certainty that the contact will occur (Garratt). A child might be capable of intent depending on age; the question is his understanding, not a categorical bar. And the intent runs to the contact, not to the harm.
cards.why: TRICKY: two distractors invite you to require purpose or to require harm-intent; both misstate the rule.

cards.scenario: At a crowded reception a guest deliberately snatches a plate from another guest's hand in a racially abusive manner, never touching his body. Can π establish a prima facie case for battery against Δ?
options: No — battery requires contact with the plaintiff's body
Yes — the person of the plaintiff includes things attached to him, such as items held or worn, under the extended person rule [Fisher]
No — only assault, since he was merely frightened
Yes — but only if the plate broke
cards.explanation: The contact must be with the person of the plaintiff, which includes things attached to him — clothing, chattels in his possession, items held or worn (Fisher, the extended person rule). Snatching a held plate is contact with the person.
cards.why: The extended person rule is the reason no skin contact is needed.

cards.scenario: A prankster pulls a chair away intending only a harmless joke. The victim falls and, because of an undiagnosed condition, suffers a catastrophic spinal injury. To what extent is Δ subject to liability?
options: Subject to liability only for the harm a normal person would have suffered
Subject to liability for all harm caused, even if unforeseeable — true of all the intentional torts
Not subject to liability, since he intended no harm
Subject to liability only if he knew of the condition
cards.explanation: The defendant is responsible for all harm caused, even if unforeseeable, and the outline notes this is true of all the intentional torts. The intent needed is intent to cause contact, not intent to cause harm.
cards.why: The eggshell principle, stated as a rule of the intentional torts generally.

cards.scenario: A doctor performs a medically flawless operation on a patient who consented to a different procedure. The patient suffers no adverse outcome. Can π establish a prima facie case for battery against Δ?
options: No — no harm resulted
Yes — the tort is complete upon contact, and good faith or a good result will not lead a court to imply consent [Mohr]
No — medical procedures are governed only by negligence
Yes — but damages are limited to nominal
cards.explanation: The tort is complete upon contact. And under Mohr, the good faith of the defendant and a good result will not be a basis for the court to imply consent, so the unconsented contact remains a battery.
cards.why: TRICKY: the absence of injury feels dispositive, but battery is complete on contact.

cards.scenario: A man taps a stranger lightly on the shoulder to ask directions. The stranger is unusually sensitive to being touched and is deeply upset. Can π establish a prima facie case for battery against Δ?
options: Yes — any unconsented touching is a battery
No — the contact intended must be harmful or offensive to a person of ordinary sensibilities, and a light tap to get attention is not
Yes — because the toucher intended the contact
No — because he did not intend to give offense
cards.explanation: The standard is objective: the contact intended must be harmful or offensive to a person with ordinary sensibilities. Intent to cause contact was present, but the contact itself does not meet the objective threshold.
cards.why: Note which distractor is closest: (d) reaches the right result by the wrong route, since intent to give offense is never required.

cards.scenario: A defendant throws a rock at A. It misses and strikes B, whom the defendant never saw. Can B establish a prima facie case for battery against Δ?
options: No — no intent as to B
Yes — intent may be transferred to another person or another cause of action [Talmage]
No — unless B was in the zone of danger
Yes — but only if A also sues
cards.explanation: Intent may be transferred to another person or to another cause of action (Talmage). The intent to commit battery against A supplies the intent element as to B, who was actually struck.
cards.why: Transferred intent is listed among the additional rules governing intent, not as a separate tort.

cards.scenario: A clerk reaches over a counter toward a customer's wife with a raised fist. Photographs later show the counter was too wide for him to have reached her. Can π establish a prima facie case for assault against Δ?
options: No — he could not physically have made contact
Yes — the defendant must have apparent ability to cause the contact, and whether he did is a question for the jury [Western Union]
No — unless she was afraid
Yes — actual ability is required and the photographs are inconclusive
cards.explanation: The requirement is apparent ability to cause the contact, and the outline flags it as a question for the jury (Western Union). Actual physical ability is not required.
cards.why: Apparent, not actual — and it is a jury question rather than a matter of law.

cards.scenario: A bodybuilder tells a smaller man, 'If you weren't my brother's friend, I'd flatten you right now,' while standing still with his arms folded. Can π establish a prima facie case for assault against Δ?
options: Yes — the threat was serious and he had the ability to carry it out
Likely no — the apprehended contact must be imminent, and words conditioned on a state of affairs that does not exist do not create expectation of imminent contact
Yes — because the words alone caused apprehension
No — because words can never constitute assault
cards.explanation: The apprehended contact must be imminent. A statement framed on a condition contrary to fact communicates that no contact is coming now, so it does not produce expectation of imminent contact.
cards.why: TRICKY: (d) states an absolute that overshoots — the defect is imminence, not that words never suffice.

cards.scenario: A veteran soldier, entirely unafraid, watches a scrawny assailant swing a bat at his head and steps aside. He sues for assault. What is the legal effect of π's lack of fear?
options: Fatal — apprehension means fear
None to the prima facie case — apprehension is best understood as expectation; fear is not required, though it may increase damages
Fatal — a plaintiff must prove emotional harm
Fatal unless he can show physical symptoms
cards.explanation: Apprehension is best understood as expectation, and the outline says fear is not required, but may increase damages. He expected the contact, which is what the element asks.
cards.why: The word 'apprehension' misleads; the outline defines it as expectation.

cards.scenario: A man sneaks up behind a woman and swings a pipe at her head, missing by inches. She never sees or hears it and learns of it a week later from a witness. Can π establish a prima facie case for assault against Δ?
options: Yes — the swing was intentional and dangerous
No — the element requires that the act cause apprehension, and the tort is complete only upon apprehension; she had none
Yes — apprehension can be established retroactively
No — but it is a battery
cards.explanation: The final element is that the act causes apprehension, and the tort is complete upon apprehension. A plaintiff who never perceived the threat experienced no expectation of contact.
cards.why: TRICKY: this is the mirror image of Parvi in false imprisonment, where awareness at the time is likewise required.

cards.scenario: A man swings at another's head intending to strike him. The victim ducks and is untouched, but saw the punch coming. What causes of action, if any, may π establish?
options: Battery only
Assault — intent to cause contact transfers to the assault cause of action, and the victim expected imminent contact
Neither, since no contact occurred and he intended contact rather than apprehension
Assault and battery both
cards.explanation: Intent may be transferred to another cause of action (Talmage), so intent to cause contact supplies the intent element for assault. The victim expected imminent harmful contact, and the tort is complete upon apprehension. No contact means no battery.
cards.why: Transfer between torts is what saves the intent element here.

cards.scenario: A store manager tells a suspected shoplifter, 'Stay right here or I'll have your car towed and call your employer.' The customer stays for an hour. No one touches her. Can π establish a prima facie case for false imprisonment against Δ?
options: No — she was free to walk out and no one restrained her
Potentially yes — physical restraint is not necessary; a threat of harm to the plaintiff, her property, or another person may be enough to confine
No — threats to property are never confinement
Yes — automatically, since she stayed
cards.explanation: Physical restraint is not necessary. Abuse of authority or a threat of harm to the plaintiff, the plaintiff's property, or another person might be enough to confine — a threat to tow her car fits that description.
cards.why: The 'stay right here or I'll...' pattern is the outline's own illustration.

cards.scenario: A guest is locked in a large walled garden with an unlocked gate on the far side that she does not know about, and no indication it exists. Was π confined within the meaning of the tort?
options: No — an available exit defeats confinement in every case
Potentially yes — the requirement is no apparent escape; an exit she has no way of knowing about is not an apparent one
No — the area was too large to be a bounded area
Yes — any enclosure is confinement regardless of exits
cards.explanation: The outline states the requirement as no apparent escape, or alternatively a risk of harm in escape. An unknown and unindicated exit is not apparent. And on size, the outline is candid: how big an area or space? We don't know.
cards.why: TRICKY: 'there was an exit' is only an answer if the exit was apparent.

cards.scenario: An intoxicated man is taken by police to a remote area and left there. He has no memory of the events afterward but was aware at the time. Is the harm-or-awareness element satisfied?
options: No — he cannot testify to what he does not remember
Yes — the element is harm or awareness, measured at the time of the confinement; later memory is a different question
No — awareness must be provable by the plaintiff's own testimony
Yes — because harm is presumed from any confinement
cards.explanation: The final element is confinement with harm or awareness, and the tort is complete upon confinement with harm or awareness. Awareness is assessed at the time; loss of memory afterward does not undo awareness that existed then.
cards.why: This is the Parvi problem: awareness at the time and memory later are distinct.

cards.scenario: A warehouse worker locks a storeroom at closing, not knowing a colleague is inside. The colleague is trapped overnight. Can π establish a prima facie case for false imprisonment against Δ?
options: Yes — the act of locking was volitional and caused confinement
No — the intent element requires intent to cause confinement or knowledge of a substantial certainty that confinement will occur, and he had neither
Yes — intent is presumed from the act
No — because the storeroom was not a bounded area
cards.explanation: The only intent necessary is the intent, or knowledge of substantial certainty, to cause confinement or that confinement will occur. A volitional act alone is not enough; without that mental state the intentional tort fails, though negligence may lie.
cards.why: Volitional act and intent are separate elements — this hypo separates them cleanly.

cards.scenario: A man could leave a locked room by climbing out a third-story window onto a narrow ledge. He stays. Was π confined within the meaning of the tort?
options: No — an escape route existed
Yes — the requirement is no apparent escape, or alternatively a risk of harm in escape; an escape that risks serious injury does not defeat confinement
No — he consented by remaining
Yes — because windows are never escapes
cards.explanation: The outline states the requirement in the alternative: no apparent escape, or risk of harm in escape. A route that would require risking a fall from a third story is not one the plaintiff must take.
cards.why: The disjunctive is easy to miss — either branch establishes the element.

cards.text: Conduct is outrageous where it is so outrageous in {{character}}, so extreme in {{degree}}, as to go beyond all possible bounds of {{decency}}, and to be regarded as {{atrocious}}, and utterly {{intolerable}} in a civilized society.
cards.why: The character and vulnerability of the victim are factors in this determination [Harris].

cards.scenario: A supervisor mocks an employee's stutter dozens of times over months. The employee testifies he was 'nervous' and 'upset,' with no other evidence of his condition. What result?
options: Recovery — the conduct was plainly outrageous
No recovery — outrageousness may be established, but severe emotional distress means a severely disabling emotional response, and vague testimony does not establish it
Recovery — severity is presumed from outrageous conduct
No recovery — mockery is never outrageous
cards.explanation: Severe emotional distress means a severely disabling emotional response by the plaintiff. Proving outrageousness does not carry the severity element, which is where these claims usually fail (Harris).
cards.why: The two elements are independent; winning one does not win the other.

cards.scenario: A plaintiff already suffering from an anxiety disorder is subjected to outrageous conduct and says it made things worse. What must π show on the severity element?
options: Nothing more — any worsening suffices
That the pre-existing condition was exacerbated by an increment that itself qualifies as severe [Harris]
That the defendant knew of the condition
That the condition was newly diagnosed
cards.explanation: Where the plaintiff has a pre-existing condition, it must be exacerbated by an increment that qualifies as severe (Harris). The baseline distress does not count toward the element.
cards.why: TRICKY: the eggshell instinct pulls toward answer (a), but the severity element is measured on the increment.

cards.scenario: A debt collector tells a debtor, 'Pay by Friday or next week my associates will break both your legs.' No violence occurs. May the threat satisfy the outrageousness element?
options: No — only completed violence is outrageous
Yes — threats of future physical violence might be sufficient [Siliznoff]
No — the threat was not imminent, so nothing is actionable
Yes — but only as assault
cards.explanation: Threats of future physical violence might be sufficient for IIED (Siliznoff). Note the contrast with assault, where the apprehended contact must be imminent; IIED has no imminence requirement.
cards.why: The lack of imminence defeats assault but not IIED — that contrast is the point.

cards.scenario: A defendant taunts a stranger about a personal tragedy he happens to know about, in a way that would leave most people unbothered but devastates this plaintiff, whose vulnerability the defendant knew. Is the victim's vulnerability relevant to the outrageousness element?
options: No — outrageousness is judged by a purely objective standard
Yes — the character and vulnerability of the victim are factors in the determination [Harris]
No — vulnerability goes only to damages
Yes — but only if the defendant is a common carrier
cards.explanation: The character and vulnerability of the victim are factors in determining outrageousness (Harris). Conduct that would be tolerable toward one person can cross the line when directed at a known vulnerability.
cards.why: Outrageousness is not assessed in a vacuum — who the victim is matters.

cards.scenario: A defendant severely beats a man in his own home while the man's daughter watches from the doorway. May the daughter establish a prima facie case for IIED?
options: Never — she was not the target
Possibly — harm to a family member in the presence of the plaintiff might be sufficient [Taylor]
Yes automatically — transferred intent supplies her claim
No — she must have been physically endangered herself
cards.explanation: Harm to a family member in the presence of the plaintiff might be sufficient (Taylor). Note the word 'might' — presence and family relationship open the door; they do not guarantee recovery, and the defendant's awareness of her presence matters.
cards.why: TRICKY: (c) overstates by invoking transferred intent, which does not simply hand a bystander an IIED claim.

cards.scenario: A factory's night operations flood a neighbor's yard with bright light and constant noise. The neighbor sues for trespass to land. What result?
options: Trespass — the light and sound physically enter the property
Not trespass — odor, light, and noise are nuisance, not trespass; trespass requires intrusion by a person or tangible substance
Trespass — because the interference is the injury
Not trespass — unless the neighbor proves damages
cards.explanation: Trespass requires intrusion by a person or tangible substance, a physical invasion. The outline expressly places odor, light, and noise in nuisance, and vibration in strict liability or nuisance.
cards.why: Classifying the intrusion is the first move — tangible or not.

cards.scenario: A hiker crosses a corner of private land, doing no damage whatsoever and leaving no trace. The owner sues. What result?
options: π cannot establish a prima facie case — no damages
Claim lies — the interference is the injury, so separate damages need not be proved, and the tort is complete upon entry
π cannot establish a prima facie case — unless the hiker was warned
Claim lies only for nominal damages if the owner proves emotional harm
cards.explanation: The interference is the injury, so separate damages need not be proved, though damages if present may be recovered. The tort is complete upon entry of the person or substance on the land.
cards.why: Contrast strict liability, where actual harm is an element.

cards.scenario: Blasting a mile away sends vibrations through the ground that shake a homeowner's foundation. He pleads trespass to land. Which statement best analyzes the claim?
options: Trespass — the vibrations physically entered the land
Not trespass — vibration is strict liability or nuisance, not trespass; but an ultrahazardous activity claim may lie since ground vibration is a characteristic risk of blasting
Trespass — because the blasting was intentional
Neither trespass nor any other claim
cards.explanation: The outline puts vibration outside trespass, assigning it to strict liability or nuisance. Vibration of the ground is expressly one of the characteristic risks that make blasting ultrahazardous, so § 519 strict liability is the right frame.
cards.why: TRICKY: the right answer requires knowing where vibration goes AND that it is a listed blasting risk.

cards.scenario: A driver, having a heart attack, loses consciousness and her car rolls onto a lawn. Can π establish a prima facie case for trespass to land against Δ?
options: Yes — her car physically entered the property
No — there is no volitional act; she was not in physical control of her actions
Yes — trespass is a strict liability tort
No — cars are not tangible substances
cards.explanation: The first element of every intentional tort is a volitional act, meaning the defendant was in physical control of her actions. Unconsciousness defeats it before any other element is reached.
cards.why: The volitional act element does the same work here it did in the seizure battery hypo.

cards.scenario: A contractor dumps a truckload of gravel just over the property line, honestly believing the line ran ten feet further. Can π establish a prima facie case for trespass to land against Δ?
options: No — he made an honest mistake about the boundary
Yes — mistake does not negate intent, and gravel is a tangible substance intruding on real property
No — unless the owner asked him to remove it and he refused
Yes — but only if the gravel caused damage
cards.explanation: Mistake as to target does not negate intent (Ransom); the same principle applies to a mistaken boundary. Gravel is a tangible substance whose intrusion interferes with the right to exclusive possession, and the interference is itself the injury.
cards.why: Two rules combine: mistake does not negate intent, and no separate damages are required.

cards.scenario: A neighbor borrows a lawnmower without permission for two hours and returns it in perfect condition. The owner did not need it and never noticed. Can π establish a prima facie case against Δ?
options: Yes — any unpermitted use is a trespass to chattels
Likely no — the interference must constitute harm to the interest in the chattel; a brief unnoticed use causing no dispossession, damage, or impairment of use does not
Yes — because the interference is itself the injury
No — because he intended to return it
cards.explanation: Unlike trespass to land, where the interference is the injury, trespass to chattels requires that the interference constitute harm to the interest in the chattel — ownership, possession, or use.
cards.why: TRICKY: (c) imports the trespass-to-land rule, which is exactly the distinction being tested.

cards.scenario: A man takes a colleague's bicycle for a week, then returns it undamaged. The colleague had to take taxis. What is the measure of damages?
options: The full value of the bicycle
Fair rental value and losses caused by impairment of use
Nominal damages only
Nothing, since the bicycle came back intact
cards.explanation: Damages for trespass to chattels are measured by the cost of repair, fair rental value, and losses caused by impairment of use, depending on the facts. Full value would be the conversion measure.
cards.why: The damages measure is what separates this tort from conversion in practice.

cards.scenario: Which of these interferences does NOT fall within the third element as stated in the outline?
options: Dispossession of the chattel
Merely touching the chattel without dispossession, damage, or impairment of use
Damage to the chattel
Impairment of use of the chattel
cards.explanation: The element lists three routes: dispossession, damage, or impairment of use. Contact alone that produces none of these does not interfere with the right of exclusive possession in the required sense.
cards.why: The three routes are exhaustive as the outline states them.

cards.scenario: A defendant lets the air out of the plaintiff's tires. The tires are undamaged and easily reinflated, but the plaintiff misses a day of work. Can π establish a prima facie case against Δ?
options: No — the chattel was not damaged or taken
Yes — impairment of use is one of the three routes, and losses caused by impairment of use are recoverable
No — this is conversion, not trespass to chattels
Yes — but recovery is limited to the cost of reinflating
cards.explanation: Impairment of use is expressly one of the three ways the interference element is satisfied, and damages include losses caused by impairment of use — here, the missed day of work.
cards.why: Impairment of use covers harms where the chattel itself is untouched.

cards.scenario: A gallery holds a painting for three days past the agreed return date, then returns it unharmed. The owner sues for conversion. Which statement best analyzes the claim?
options: Conversion — any unauthorized retention is conversion
Likely trespass to chattels rather than conversion — conversion requires permanent or very long term dispossession or substantial destruction such as would warrant payment of full value
Neither, since the painting came back
Conversion — because paintings are unique
cards.explanation: Conversion requires interference by permanent or very long term dispossession or impairment of use, or substantial destruction, such as would warrant payment by the defendant of the full value of the chattel. A three-day delay is far short of that; trespass to chattels is the fit.
cards.why: The two chattel torts differ in degree, and § 222A's factors mark the line.

cards.text: Conversion is an intentional exercise of {{dominion}} or {{control}} over a chattel which so seriously interferes with the right of another to control it that the actor may justly be required to pay the other the {{full}} {{value}} of the chattel.
cards.why: Subsection (2) supplies six factors for measuring the seriousness of the interference.

cards.prompt: Name the six § 222A(2) factors for determining the seriousness of the interference.
answer: (a) The extent and duration of the actor's exercise of dominion or control;
(b) the actor's intent to assert a right in fact inconsistent with the other's right of control;
(c) the actor's good faith;
