(d) the extent and duration of the resulting interference with the other's right of control;
(e) the harm done to the chattel;
(f) the inconvenience and expense caused to the other.
cards.fallback: Extent and {{duration}} of the exercise of dominion; the actor's {{intent}} to assert an inconsistent right; the actor's {{good}} faith; the extent and duration of the resulting {{interference}}; the {{harm}} done to the chattel; and the {{inconvenience}} and expense caused to the other.
cards.why: No single factor is predominant — the question is one of degree, which is why conversion and trespass to chattels sit on a spectrum.

cards.scenario: A defendant takes the plaintiff's car and sells it to an unknown buyer who cannot be traced. Does π's claim lie in trespass to chattels or in conversion?
options: Trespass to chattels — he did not destroy the car
Conversion — permanent dispossession warranting payment of the full value
Neither — the buyer is the proper defendant
Conversion only if he acted in bad faith
cards.explanation: Conversion requires interference by permanent or very long term dispossession or substantial destruction, such as would warrant payment of the full value of the chattel. An untraceable sale permanently deprives the owner.
cards.why: The remedy defines the tort: full value is the marker of conversion.

cards.scenario: A warehouse in complete good faith delivers the plaintiff's goods to the wrong claimant, who consumes them. The warehouse pleads its good faith. What result under § 222A?
options: Complete defense — good faith negates the intent element
Not a defense, though it is one of the six factors bearing on the seriousness of the interference; the goods are gone, so the other factors point to conversion
Complete defense — conversion requires bad faith
Irrelevant in every respect
cards.explanation: The actor's good faith is factor (c) under § 222A(2) — one consideration among six, not an answer to the claim. Where the extent of the dispossession is total and the harm complete, good faith will not carry the day.
cards.why: TRICKY: good faith appears in the rule, which makes it tempting to treat as a defense; it is only a factor.

cards.scenario: Under § 222A(2), which of these is NOT one of the listed factors?
options: The extent and duration of the actor's exercise of dominion or control
Whether the actor was negligent in acquiring the chattel
The harm done to the chattel
The inconvenience and expense caused to the other
cards.explanation: The six factors are extent and duration of dominion; intent to assert an inconsistent right; good faith; extent and duration of the resulting interference; harm done to the chattel; and inconvenience and expense to the other. Negligence in acquisition is not among them — conversion is an intentional tort.
cards.why: TRICKY: negligence sounds plausible in a list of factors but has no place in an intentional tort.

cards.scenario: A defendant intentionally destroys the plaintiff's laptop with a hammer. Which route to conversion applies, and what is the measure of recovery?
options: Long term dispossession; fair rental value
Substantial destruction; payment of the full value of the chattel, plus incidental losses
Impairment of use; cost of repair
No conversion, since he never possessed it
cards.explanation: Substantial destruction is one of the routes to conversion, and the remedy is payment of the full value of the chattel to the rightful possessor, with incidental losses also recoverable.
cards.why: Destruction is a route that requires no dispossession at all.

cards.scenario: Two defendants each keep the plaintiff's identical tools for a month. One returns them; the other cannot because they were stolen from his shed. Do both Δs commit the same tort?
options: Yes — both interfered for the same duration
No — duration is only one § 222A factor; the resulting interference differs, and only the second produced a loss warranting payment of full value
Yes — both are conversions because both exceeded a reasonable time
No — the second defendant has a defense because the theft was not his fault
cards.explanation: Section 222A(2) weighs several factors, including the extent and duration of the exercise of dominion AND the extent and duration of the resulting interference and the harm done. Identical durations can still produce different results where one interference ends in total loss.
cards.why: The factors are not a checklist of one variable; consequences matter alongside conduct.

cards.scenario: A jury finds the plaintiff proved every element of battery AND that the defendant proved consent. What result?
options: Plaintiff wins — the prima facie case was established
Defendant wins — if both are established, the affirmative defense defeats the plaintiff's prima facie case
The claims cancel and each bears its own costs
A new trial is required
cards.explanation: Where both the prima facie case and the affirmative defense are established, the affirmative defense defeats the plaintiff's prima facie case. That is what makes it affirmative rather than a denial.
cards.why: The defense does not negate an element; it overcomes a case that was fully made out.

cards.scenario: A defendant never pleads self-defense but raises it for the first time in closing argument. Is there a defect in Δ's position?
options: None — evidence at trial is what matters
Yes — affirmative defenses must be pleaded and proved by the defendant under FRCP 8 and similar state rules
None — self-defense is not an affirmative defense
Yes — but only in federal court
cards.explanation: Affirmative defenses must be pleaded and proved by the defendant, under FRCP 8 and similar state procedural rules. Both halves of that requirement matter — pleading and proof.
cards.why: The burden allocation is the practical heart of the affirmative-defense concept.

cards.scenario: A surgeon has consent to operate on the right ear. Under anesthesia he discovers the left ear is worse, operates on it in good faith, and the result is excellent. Does the affirmative defense of consent attach?
options: Yes — the good result cures any defect in consent
No — the scope of consent may not be exceeded, and the good faith of the defendant and a good result will not be a basis to imply consent [Mohr]
Yes — consent to ear surgery covers both ears
No — but only because he failed to wake the patient and ask
cards.explanation: Two rules from Mohr converge: the scope of consent may not be exceeded, and the good faith of the defendant and a good result will not be a basis for a court to imply consent.
cards.why: The outline's own illustration, and the reason Mohr is assigned.

cards.scenario: A football player is struck in the back of the head well after the whistle, a blow no rule permits. He sues. The defender pleads consent to the violence of the sport. What result?
options: Consent bars the claim — football is a violent sport
Consent is limited to contact within the customs of the sport or activity, which may go beyond the rules of the game but does not reach a deliberate strike after play has ended [Hackbart]
Consent bars the claim because he signed a waiver
Consent never applies to professional athletes
cards.explanation: Consent is limited to contact or otherwise tortious activity within the customs of the sport or activity (Hackbart), and the outline notes this may go beyond the rules of the game. Custom, not the rulebook, marks the boundary — and a blow after the whistle is outside it.
cards.why: TRICKY: 'may go beyond the rules of the game' cuts both ways — custom is broader than the rules but still bounded.

cards.scenario: An immigrant in a vaccination line holds up her arm to the doctor without a word, having watched others do the same. She later sues for battery. Which form of consent is presented?
options: Express, because she moved deliberately
Apparent — a gesture or behavior indicating consent as it would be understood by a reasonable person under all the circumstances, including in some cases silence [O'Brien]
Implied, since the court supplies it from the nature of her activity
No consent at all, since she said nothing
cards.explanation: Apparent consent is a gesture or behavior by the plaintiff communicating or otherwise indicating consent, as it would be understood by a reasonable person under all the circumstances, including in some cases the plaintiff's silence (O'Brien). Express consent requires a clear expression, spoken or written.
cards.why: Apparent and implied often overlap; O'Brien is the apparent-consent case.

cards.scenario: A man conceals a communicable disease he has a duty to disclose and obtains his partner's agreement to contact. What is the legal effect on the consent given?
options: Valid — she agreed to the contact that occurred

Invalid — consent obtained by deceit, misrepresentation, or silence concerning a matter as to which there is a duty to disclose is vitiated by the failure to disclose information material to the consent
Valid unless she asked and he lied
Invalid only if she contracts the disease
cards.explanation: Consent is invalid if obtained by deceit, misrepresentation, or silence concerning a matter as to which there is a duty to disclose; it is vitiated by failure to disclose information material to the consent. Silence is expressly included.
cards.why: Note that silence can vitiate consent as readily as an affirmative lie.

cards.scenario: Paramedics treat an unconscious accident victim who would die without immediate care. Nothing suggests he would refuse. What conditions must be satisfied before a provider may treat without consent?
options: None — emergencies suspend all consent requirements
The patient is unable to consent; delay imposes a risk of serious harm; a reasonable person would consent; and the provider has no reason to believe this patient would refuse
Only that the patient is unconscious
Only that a reasonable person would consent
cards.explanation: All four conditions are stated together: inability to consent because unconscious, incompetent, seriously intoxicated, or mentally ill; risk of serious harm if treatment is delayed; a reasonable person would consent under the circumstances; and no reason to believe this particular patient would refuse.
cards.why: The fourth condition is the one people forget — a known refusal, such as a religious objection, controls.

cards.scenario: A man knocks his attacker to the ground, ending the threat. He then kicks the attacker twice more while he lies there. Does the privilege attach to Δ's conduct?
options: Yes — he was originally attacked
No as to the kicks — there is no privilege to retaliate, and only such force as is necessary in the circumstances is privileged
Yes — doubts are resolved in favor of the defendant
No — self-defense requires retreat first
cards.explanation: There is no privilege to retaliate, and only such force as is necessary in the circumstances is privileged. Once the threat ended, the privilege ended with it.
cards.why: Self-defense is forward-looking; retaliation is not defense.

cards.scenario: A man reasonably but wrongly believes an approaching stranger is about to attack him, and shoves him away. The stranger was reaching to hand him a dropped wallet. Does the privilege attach to Δ's conduct?
options: No — he was mistaken about the threat
Yes — the privilege is present when the defendant reasonably believes the use of force in self-defense is necessary, even if he is mistaken
No — unless the stranger appeared armed
Yes — but only if he apologizes
cards.explanation: The privilege turns on reasonable belief, and it is expressly available even where the defendant is mistaken. Reasonableness, not accuracy, is the test.
cards.why: Compare defense of others, where courts are divided on mistake.

cards.scenario: A man is subjected to an extraordinary stream of racial and personal abuse. He punches the speaker. Does the privilege of self-defense attach to Δ's conduct?
options: Yes — the abuse was outrageous
No — insults, no matter how vile, do not create a privilege to use force; that is not self-defense at common law
Yes — words can constitute a threat of battery
No — but the abuse reduces damages
cards.explanation: Insults, no matter how vile, do not create a privilege to use force. The outline is emphatic on this point: it is not self-defense at common law.
cards.why: TRICKY: the conduct may support an IIED claim BY the punched party's victim, but it never licenses a punch.

cards.scenario: A woman is threatened in her own kitchen by an intruder. She could safely leave through the back door but stands her ground and uses force. Does the privilege attach to Δ's conduct?
options: No — she was required to retreat because escape was safe
Yes — retreat is not required in one's home
No — retreat is always required at common law
Yes — but only in states following the majority rule
cards.explanation: Retreat is not required in one's home. At common law retreat was required elsewhere; today a majority of states do not require retreat anywhere, and a minority do.
cards.why: The home exception held even under the stricter common law rule.

cards.scenario: A man sees another draw back a fist. Before the blow lands he strikes first. The other argues no battery had yet occurred. What result?
options: No privilege — self-defense requires an actual battery first
Privilege available — there is no need to wait for an actual battery to occur before acting in self-defense
No privilege — striking first is always retaliation
Privilege only if he first shouted a warning
cards.explanation: There is no need for the defendant to wait for an actual battery to occur before acting in self-defense. The privilege attaches to a reasonably perceived threat.
cards.why: Pairs with the reasonable-belief rule: the law does not require absorbing the first blow.

cards.scenario: A bystander sees a man being beaten and intervenes with force. It turns out the man being beaten had started the fight and was the aggressor. What result?
options: Privileged in every jurisdiction — he acted reasonably
Uncertain — the privilege is derivative of the other's privilege, and on mistake the courts are divided
Never privileged — mistake destroys the defense
Privileged, because doubts are resolved in favor of the defendant
cards.explanation: Defense of others is a privilege derivative of the other person's privilege to defend himself. If the person defended had no privilege because he was the aggressor, the intervenor's derivative privilege is problematic — and the outline notes courts are divided on mistake.
cards.why: TRICKY: self-defense expressly protects reasonable mistake; defense of others does not clearly do so.

cards.scenario: An intervenor uses far more force than the person he is defending could lawfully have used. What result?
options: Privileged — intervenors get latitude
Not privileged as to the excess — the intervenor's conduct is governed by all the same rules that govern the victim's in self-defense
Privileged if he acted in good faith
Not privileged at all, since only the victim may defend himself
cards.explanation: The intervenor's conduct is governed by all the same rules as govern the victim's in cases of self-defense, including that only such force as is necessary in the circumstances is privileged.
cards.why: Derivative means it inherits both the scope and the limits.

cards.scenario: An owner rigs a spring gun in a boarded-up farmhouse to stop trespassers. It shoots a trespasser in the leg. Does the privilege attach to Δ's conduct?
options: Yes — he was defending his property from an unlawful intrusion
No — deadly force may not be used to protect property, and one may not use a mechanical device to do what one could not do oneself [Katko]
Yes — because he posted warning signs
No — but only because the trespasser was unarmed
cards.explanation: Both rules from Katko apply: deadly force may not be used to protect property, and one may not use a mechanical device to do what one could not do in person.
cards.why: The mechanical-device rule prevents evading the deadly force limit by automation.

cards.scenario: A homeowner shoves a meter reader off the porch, telling him to stay off the property. The meter reader had a legal right of entry. Does the privilege attach to Δ's conduct?
options: Yes — it is his property
No — there is no privilege to use force if the intrusion onto the property is lawful
Yes — provided the force was non-deadly
No — unless he first asked him to leave
cards.explanation: There is no privilege to use force where the intrusion onto property is lawful. The outline gives the meter reader and the postal carrier as the examples.
cards.why: The privilege presupposes a tort against the property; a lawful entry is not one.

cards.scenario: An intruder breaks into an occupied home at night while the family is inside. Which framework governs the occupants' use of force?
options: Defense of property, so deadly force is barred
A different framework — unlawful entry into an occupied home is a threat to the occupiers, conceptually different and governed by different rules, with the Castle Doctrine applying
Defense of others only
Necessity
cards.explanation: The outline expressly separates this case: unlawful entry into an occupied home is a threat to the occupiers, conceptually different from defense of property and governed by different rules. The Castle Doctrine applies there.
cards.why: TRICKY: the Katko bar on deadly force applies to property, not to a threat against occupants of an occupied home.

cards.scenario: An owner keeps a dog trained to attack anyone entering the yard. It mauls a trespasser. What result under Katko?
options: Privileged — a dog is not a mechanical device
Not privileged — one may not use a mechanical device OR a dog to do what one could not do oneself
Privileged if the dog was leashed
Not privileged only if the owner was present
cards.explanation: Katko's rule as stated in the outline covers both: one may not use a mechanical device or dog to do what one could not do oneself. The outline flags that this may defy common sense but is the rule.
cards.why: The professor specifically noted the dog cases as counterintuitive — see the outline's note.

cards.scenario: A shopkeeper sees a customer walking out with an unpaid item and blocks the door with his body, using no more force than needed. Does the privilege attach to Δ's conduct?
options: No — any force to protect property is barred
Yes — one may use reasonable, non-deadly force to prevent the commission of a tort against one's property
No — he should have called the police
Yes — but only under the Castle Doctrine
cards.explanation: The general rule permits reasonable force to prevent the commission of a tort against one's property. Only deadly force is categorically barred.
cards.why: Reasonable force is permitted; the line is deadly force.

cards.scenario: A man sees his stolen bicycle chained outside a cafe. He waits, and when the taker emerges he demands it back. The taker refuses and mounts the bike. Does the privilege to recapture the chattel attach?
options: No — self-help is never permitted
Yes — the rightful possessor may use non-deadly force to recapture after a demand for return is ignored, if he reasonably believes it can be recovered only by such force
Yes — including deadly force, since it is his property
No — he must sue in conversion
cards.explanation: Under § 77 the rightful possessor may use non-deadly force to recapture the chattel after a demand for return is ignored, provided he reasonably believes the chattel can be recovered only by the use of such force.
cards.why: The demand requirement is the default; the other two branches are exceptions to it.

cards.scenario: A thief is running away with a woman's laptop. She does not shout a demand — there is plainly no point — and tackles him. Does the privilege attach to Δ's conduct?
options: No — she skipped the required demand
Yes — a demand is excused if the rightful possessor reasonably believes such demand would be useless, or that substantial harm could be done to the chattel before demand can be made
No — unless she first called the police
Yes — but only if the laptop was damaged
cards.explanation: Section 77 excuses the demand where the rightful possessor reasonably believes it would be useless, or reasonably believes substantial harm could be done to the chattel before a demand can be made.
cards.why: Three routes in: demand ignored, demand useless, or harm imminent.

cards.scenario: A store manager, on reasonable suspicion of shoplifting, detains a customer in an office for six hours without contacting anyone. Does the privilege attach to Δ's conduct?
options: Yes — reasonable suspicion existed
No as to the duration — detention is privileged only for a reasonable amount of time to investigate
Yes — because he used no force at all
No — the privilege does not exist at common law
cards.explanation: The privilege permits detention on the premises for a reasonable amount of time to investigate. Reasonable suspicion opens the door but does not license indefinite detention.
cards.why: Each component of the privilege carries its own reasonableness limit.

cards.scenario: A merchant, suspecting theft, follows a customer four blocks down the street and detains her there. Does the privilege attach to Δ's conduct?
options: Yes — pursuit is permitted so long as suspicion is reasonable
No — the privilege as stated permits detention on the premises
Yes — because the chattel was still in her possession
No — because he did not first demand return
cards.explanation: The common law privilege as stated permits a retail merchant to use reasonable force to detain the customer on the premises. The outline notes most states now regulate this by statute, but this course concerns the common law form.
cards.why: TRICKY: modern statutes often extend to the immediate vicinity — the outline tells you to use the common law version.

cards.scenario: Who decides whether a shopkeeper's suspicion, force, and detention time were reasonable?
options: The jury alone, in all cases
The court in the first instance, then the jury
The court alone, as a matter of law
The merchant, subject to review
cards.explanation: The determination of what is reasonable is for the court in the first instance, then for the jury. The court screens; the jury decides what survives the screen.
cards.why: This allocation is stated expressly in the outline.

cards.scenario: A city official orders houses demolished to create a firebreak, saving the rest of the town. An owner sues. What result at common law?
options: Recovery of the full value of the house
No compensation required at common law under public necessity, though many states now provide for it by statute
Recovery limited to the value of the land
Recovery of the house plus punitive damages
cards.explanation: Public necessity requires no compensation at common law; the rationale may have been that this particular property would have been destroyed anyway. Many states have since provided for compensation by statute (Surocco).
cards.why: Public necessity is a complete defense — the contrast with private necessity is the compensation.

cards.scenario: A ship captain moors to a private dock during a violent storm to save the ship and crew. The ship damages the dock. Is Δ subject to liability, and to what extent?
options: None — necessity is a complete defense
The user must pay the value of the damage to the dock, but no punitive damages — private necessity is an incomplete defense
Full liability for trespass plus punitive damages
None, because the dock owner could not have compelled him to leave
cards.explanation: Private necessity is an incomplete defense (Lake Erie Transport). No legal wrong is committed, so the owner cannot compel the user to desist, but the user must still pay the value of any damage — without punitive damages.
cards.why: 'Incomplete' is doing precise work: it defeats the tort but not the compensation.

cards.scenario: During that same storm, the dock owner unties the ship's lines and casts it off. The ship is wrecked. Is Δ subject to liability, and to what extent?
options: None — it was his dock and he may exclude anyone
The owner is subject to liability — if the owner forces the user to desist and harm results to the user or the user's property, the owner is subject to liability
None, unless he acted maliciously
The owner is subject to liability only for the value of the mooring
cards.explanation: Because no legal wrong is committed by the privileged user, the owner may not compel him to desist; and if the owner does force him to desist and harm results to the user or the user's property, the owner is subject to liability.
cards.why: This is the flip side of Lake Erie Transport, and the reason the privilege is meaningful.

cards.scenario: Health officials confine residents of a building during an outbreak. The residents sue for false imprisonment. On what affirmative defense should Δ rely?
options: Consent, since they live there
Public necessity — the principle includes quarantine and other physical restraints that would otherwise be false imprisonment or battery
Private necessity, with compensation owed
No defense exists; false imprisonment is strict
cards.explanation: The outline expressly extends public necessity to quarantine and other physical restraints that would otherwise constitute false imprisonment or battery, and it is a defense to all the intentional torts studied.
cards.why: Public necessity is not confined to property destruction cases.

cards.scenario: A firefighter destroys a shed that is not yet burning, reasonably believing it will spread flames to a school. It turns out the shed was fireproof and posed no risk. What affirmative defense, if any, is available to Δ?
options: No — the destruction was in fact unnecessary
Yes — property may be destroyed when necessary, OR APPARENTLY NECESSARY, to prevent great harm to the community
No — unless the school actually caught fire
Yes — but compensation is required because he was mistaken
cards.explanation: The rule reaches conduct necessary or apparently necessary to prevent great harm to the community. Apparent necessity suffices, and public necessity requires no compensation at common law.
cards.why: TRICKY: hindsight makes the destruction look gratuitous, but the standard is assessed on apparent necessity.

cards.scenario: A defendant's conduct fits no named privilege, but the circumstances were extraordinary and his response was measured. Is any affirmative defense available to Δ?
options: No — the privileges are a closed list
Possibly justification — a catch-all under Rest. 2d § 10 recognizing that a privilege may arise in circumstances unanticipated before [Sindle]
Only public necessity
Only consent, if implied
cards.explanation: Justification is a catch-all concept under Restatement (2d) § 10: a privilege to commit an otherwise tortious act may arise in various circumstances unanticipated before. The categories of privilege are not carved in stone.
cards.why: The point of Sindle in the syllabus is precisely this flexibility.

cards.scenario: What test did Sindle apply?
options: The § 520 abnormally dangerous factors
A measure of necessity — the concept, not the defense — under the particular circumstances
The Learned Hand formula
Reasonable suspicion, as in the shopkeeper's privilege
cards.explanation: The outline states that the test in Sindle is simply a measure of necessity under those particular circumstances, and specifically flags that this means the concept of necessity rather than the necessity defense.
cards.why: TRICKY: the word 'necessity' appears, but this is not the necessity defense.

cards.scenario: How is the general duty in negligence stated?
options: To avoid all foreseeable harm to anyone
A legal obligation to act as an ordinary, reasonable, prudent person under all circumstances
To use the utmost care in every activity
To comply with all applicable statutes
cards.explanation: The general duty is a legal obligation to act as an ordinary, reasonable, prudent person under all circumstances. Statutes and customs are sources that may supply the content of a duty, not the general formulation.
cards.why: Distinguish the general duty from the sources that give it content.

cards.scenario: A defendant with a significantly below-average IQ fails to appreciate an obvious risk. What standard applies?
options: A reasonable person of similar intelligence
The ordinary reasonable person — low IQ does not lower the standard
A subjective standard based on his actual capacities
The child standard, by analogy
cards.explanation: Among the mental caveats, low IQ receives no allowance: the standard remains the ordinary reasonable person. Contrast physical limitations, which are accounted for.
cards.why: Physical limitations are accommodated; mental ones generally are not.

cards.scenario: A blind pedestrian, walking without noticing a hazard visible only to sighted people, injures another. What standard of care governs Δ's conduct?
options: The ordinary reasonable sighted person
The duty of a reasonable blind person to others — physical limitations are accounted for
A subjective standard based on his own habits
Strict liability
cards.explanation: Physical limitations are accounted for: the outline frames it as the duty of a reasonable blind or deaf person, or a reasonable wheelchair-bound person, to others.
cards.why: The contrast with low IQ and insanity is the point of the list.

cards.scenario: An experienced pharmacologist, acting in an ordinary personal capacity, recognizes a drug interaction that a layperson would miss, and says nothing. What standard of care governs Δ's conduct?
options: The ordinary reasonable person, who would not have known
He must use his superior knowledge
The professional standard only if he was on duty
A subjective standard of his own choosing
cards.explanation: Among the caveats, superior knowledge is the one that raises the bar: a person with superior knowledge must use that knowledge.
cards.why: Superior knowledge is the mirror image of 'lacking knowledge,' which gets no allowance either way.

cards.scenario: A twelve-year-old shoots a friend while handling a rifle carelessly. What standard of care governs Δ's conduct?
options: That of a child of like age, education, intelligence and experience
The adult standard — a gun is always the adult standard
A subjective standard based on this child's actual maturity
Strict liability
cards.explanation: When conducting dangerous activities generally reserved for adults, children are held to an adult standard. The outline says there is no clear rule and to look at the thing the child is using — but that a gun is always the adult standard.
cards.why: The gun rule is the one bright line in an otherwise fuzzy area.

cards.scenario: A child defendant argues the standard should account for his own unusual immaturity relative to other children his age. What result?
options: Accepted — the standard is subjective as to children
Rejected — the standard is objective: based on children with characteristics similar to those of this child, but not on this particular child
Accepted only if supported by expert testimony
Rejected — children are always held to the adult standard
cards.explanation: The child standard is objective. It is a general standard based on children with characteristics similar to those of this child — like age, education, intelligence and experience — but it is not based on this particular child.
cards.why: TRICKY: 'like age, education, intelligence and experience' sounds individualized, but the outline stresses it remains objective.

cards.scenario: A ten-year-old riding a bicycle collides with a pedestrian. What standard of care governs Δ's conduct?
options: Adult — bicycles are vehicles
Child standard — bicycles fall on the side of activities not generally reserved for adults, unlike a tractor, snowmobile, or gun
Adult — any activity causing injury triggers the adult standard
Strict liability
cards.explanation: There is no clear rule; the outline says to look at the thing the child is using and contrasts a tractor, snowmobile, or gun with small toys, a ball, or a bicycle. A bicycle falls on the child-standard side.
cards.why: The comparison list in the outline is the closest thing to guidance here.

cards.scenario: A defendant proves he complied with every custom of his industry. What is the legal effect of that showing?
options: Complete defense — compliance with custom establishes due care
Important evidence that courts ordinarily follow, but it does not bind the court or jury and may be challenged on Hand Formula considerations [Helling v. Carey]
Irrelevant — custom is inadmissible
Conclusive only if the custom is written
cards.explanation: Custom is evidence of the content of a duty a particular industry imposes on itself. It does not bind court or jury but is important evidence, and courts ordinarily follow it — though it may be challenged on Hand Formula grounds, as in Helling v. Carey.
cards.why: TRICKY: 'courts ordinarily follow it' invites treating custom as conclusive; Helling is the counterexample.

cards.scenario: An entire profession follows a custom of not administering a cheap, safe test to younger patients. A young patient is harmed by the undetected condition. Basis for challenging the custom?
options: None — the profession sets its own standard
Hand Formula considerations — where the burden of the precaution is small relative to the risk, the custom may be found inadequate [Helling v. Carey]
Negligence per se
Res ipsa loquitur
cards.explanation: Custom may be challenged on the basis of Hand Formula considerations, and Helling v. Carey is the outline's example: a cheap precaution against a serious risk can render an entire custom insufficient.
cards.why: Helling is why custom is evidence rather than a safe harbor.

cards.prompt: Name the five categories of excused violation under § 288A(2).
answer: An excused violation of a legislative enactment or an administrative regulation is not negligence.
Unless the enactment or regulation is construed not to permit such excuse, its violation is excused when:
(a) the violation is reasonable because of the actor's incapacity;
(b) he neither knows nor should know of the occasion for compliance;
(c) he is unable after reasonable diligence or care to comply;
(d) he is confronted by an emergency not due to his own misconduct;
(e) compliance would involve a greater risk of harm to the actor or to others.
cards.fallback: Violation reasonable because of the actor's {{incapacity}}; he neither {{knows}} nor should know of the occasion for compliance; unable after reasonable {{diligence}} to comply; confronted by an {{emergency}} not due to his own misconduct; compliance would involve a greater {{risk}} of harm.
cards.why: The outline flags (e) as the most important: obedience to the statute would be more dangerous than disobedience.

cards.scenario: A statute requires fencing around livestock to prevent animals wandering onto highways. A farmer's unfenced sheep contract a disease from a neighbor's herd. Does negligence per se apply?
options: Yes — the statute was violated and harm followed
No — the statute must protect against injury of the type suffered; disease is not the highway-collision harm the statute targets
Yes — the farmer is in the protected class
No — because the statute did not mention disease explicitly
cards.explanation: Both requirements must be met: the statute must protect a class of persons including the plaintiff AND protect from injury of the type suffered. Failing the type-of-harm requirement, negligence per se cannot be applied and the case proceeds as common law negligence.
cards.why: The two-part screen is where most negligence per se questions are decided.

cards.scenario: Negligence per se does not apply because the type-of-harm requirement fails. What happens to the plaintiff's case?
options: It is dismissed
Treat the cause of action as common law negligence; the statute may still be useful as a source of ideas for the content of duty, but need not be adopted per se
It converts to strict liability
The jury is instructed to disregard the statute entirely
cards.explanation: The outline is explicit: in such a case, treat the cause of action as common law negligence. The statute might still be useful as a source of ideas for the content of duty, and breach, cause in fact, and proximate cause are applied as they would ordinarily be.
cards.why: Failing negligence per se is not failing the case.

cards.scenario: A driver crosses a double yellow line — a statutory violation — to avoid a child who has run into the roadway. Sued by an oncoming motorist. Best argument?
options: No violation occurred
The violation is excused: compliance would have involved a greater risk of harm, the most important excuse under § 288A
The statute does not protect motorists
Negligence per se never applies to traffic statutes
cards.explanation: Negligence per se binds the jury on duty and breach unless obedience to the statute is excused. Excuse may be adopted from the § 288A list, and the outline flags as most important that obedience to the statute would be more dangerous than disobedience.
cards.why: Excuse operates even where both threshold requirements are satisfied.

cards.scenario: Negligence per se applies and the violation is unexcused. What has the plaintiff established?
options: The entire prima facie case
Duty and breach — it binds the jury on those; the violation must still be a cause in fact and a proximate cause of the harm
Duty only
Liability, subject only to damages
cards.explanation: Negligence per se binds the jury on duty and breach unless obedience is excused. The violation must also be a cause in fact of the harm, and a proximate cause — though proximate cause is rarely an issue in these cases.
cards.why: TRICKY: 'per se' sounds like it decides everything; it decides two elements.

cards.scenario: Why is proximate cause rarely contested in negligence per se cases?
options: Because statutes eliminate the requirement
Because by the nature of negligence per se, the plaintiff is a foreseeable plaintiff suffering a foreseeable harm
Because the jury is bound on all elements
Because cause in fact subsumes it
cards.explanation: The outline explains it directly: proximate cause is rarely an issue because by the nature of negligence per se the plaintiff is a foreseeable plaintiff suffering a foreseeable harm — which is precisely what the two threshold requirements establish.
cards.why: The two requirements do double duty, screening entry and resolving foreseeability.

cards.scenario: A rural physician argues he should be judged against the practices of other physicians in his small town. What result?
options: Correct — the locality rule governs
Incorrect — for physicians the standard of care is national; the old locality rule is out
Correct if no specialists practice nearby
Incorrect only for specialists
cards.explanation: For physicians the standard of care is national. The outline states flatly that the old locality rule is out.
cards.why: A clean, testable rule with no qualifiers attached.

cards.scenario: A surgeon performs a procedure flawlessly within the standard of care, but never warned of a known 2% risk of nerve damage that materializes. On what theory does π's claim proceed?
options: Battery, since the patient did not consent to nerve damage
Negligence — informed consent is part of the physician's duty and standard of care, and failure to inform is handled as negligence, not battery
Strict liability
π cannot establish a prima facie case — the treatment met the standard of care
cards.explanation: Informed consent is part of the physician's duty and standard of care, and the outline is explicit that failure to inform is handled as negligence, not battery, in Franklin and generally in the US. It is precisely the theory used when treatment was properly performed but an adverse outcome followed.
cards.why: TRICKY: unconsented touching sounds like battery, but the doctrine is deliberately framed in negligence.

cards.scenario: By what measure is the materiality of a risk judged for informed consent?
options: What a reasonable physician would disclose
Those facts that would be material to a reasonable patient in the same situation as the plaintiff-patient
What this particular patient says she would have wanted
Whatever the hospital's consent form lists
cards.explanation: The outline states the measure as those facts that would be material to a reasonable patient in the same situation as the plaintiff-patient — a patient-centered rather than physician-centered standard.
cards.why: Note the standard is reasonable-patient, not reasonable-physician.

cards.scenario: A plaintiff sues an electrician for negligence and offers no expert testimony on the trade's standards. Is there a defect in Δ's position?
options: None — juries apply common sense to all cases
Yes — for a professional or person with special skill, expert testimony is generally necessary
None — electricians are held to the ordinary reasonable person standard
Yes — but only in medical cases
cards.explanation: Where the professional standard applies — physician, specialist, attorney, pilot, electrician — the defendant must possess and exercise the knowledge and skill of an ordinary member of the profession in good standing, and expert testimony is generally necessary to establish it.
cards.why: The outline lists electrician among the examples, which is easy to overlook.

cards.scenario: A neurologist is sued. Against whom is she measured?
options: Any licensed physician
An ordinary member of her profession or occupation in good standing — here, the specialty
The most skilled neurologist available
A reasonable person with no medical training
cards.explanation: The standard is possession and exercise of the knowledge and skill of an ordinary member of the profession or occupation in good standing. The outline lists specialists — neurologist, psychiatrist — separately, so the comparison group is the specialty.
cards.why: Ordinary member in good standing, not the best in the field.

cards.scenario: A driver has a seizure, crashes through an unbarricaded roadside work zone, and injures a worker. The contractor argues the driver's conduct was the cause. Did Δ owe π a duty on these facts?
options: No duty — the driver's negligence was an intervening cause
Duty exists — the foreseeable negligence of one tortfeasor can become the basis of a duty imposed on another; negligent driving is foreseeable at a roadside site [Derdiarian]
No duty — contractors owe duties only to their own employees
Duty exists only if the contractor knew this driver was ill
cards.explanation: Sometimes the foreseeable negligence of one tortfeasor becomes the basis of a duty imposed on another. Derdiarian is the outline's example: the general contractor had a duty to put barriers up precisely because negligent driving is foreseeable.
cards.why: The foreseeability of the other party's negligence is what creates the duty, not what excuses it.

cards.scenario: A tenant is assaulted in a building where assaults have occurred repeatedly and the locks are broken. Did the landlord owe π a duty on these facts?
options: None — the criminal, not the landlord, caused the harm
A duty to provide security sufficient for the risk, such as locks and cameras, based on the foreseeability of intentional torts and crimes in that place
A duty to insure tenants against all crime
None, unless the landlord invited the assailant
cards.explanation: The outline recognizes a landlord's duty to provide security sufficient for the risk — locks, cameras — based on the foreseeability of intentional torts and crimes in that place, and notes the extent of the duty depends on the risk.
cards.why: 'Sufficient for the risk' is the calibration: the duty scales with foreseeability.

cards.scenario: Facts fit no statute, custom, or precedent. What is the method for identifying a possible duty?
options: Conclude there is no duty
Reverse engineer: review the sequence from the defendant's conduct to the harm, identify what he could have done differently to prevent it, and treat that conduct as the possible duty
Apply strict liability
Ask whether the defendant acted in good faith
cards.explanation: The outline prescribes reviewing the sequence of facts from conduct to harm, determining what the defendant could have done differently, and treating whatever conduct would have prevented the harm as the possible duty — noting that its cost becomes the cost of avoidance under Hand.
cards.why: The method deliberately feeds into the Hand formula's second variable.

cards.scenario: From what vantage point is the Hand analysis conducted?
options: With hindsight, knowing the harm that actually occurred
Metaphorically at the place where, and the time just before, the conduct took place — looking forward
At the time of trial
From the plaintiff's perspective at the moment of injury
cards.explanation: The outline directs you to put yourself metaphorically at the place where, and at the time just before, the conduct took place, and then to look forward at likelihood and severity as they would have been understood then.
cards.why: Ex ante, not ex post — the harm that happened is not the measure.

cards.scenario: Which two considerations together constitute the RISK side of the comparison?
options: Cost to the defendant and cost to society
The likelihood that some harm would occur, and the likely severity of that harm should it occur
Foreseeability and proximate cause
The custom of the industry and the applicable statute
cards.explanation: The outline groups them expressly: the likelihood, as understood then, that some harm would occur, and the likely severity of that harm should it occur — 1 and 2 together are the RISK.
cards.why: The pairing is stated on the page; the cost of avoidance sits on the other side.

cards.scenario: Whose costs are weighed on the avoidance side?
options: Only this defendant's out-of-pocket cost
The cost to this defendant, the cost to others similarly situated, and the social costs, if any, of imposing the duty
Only the plaintiff's cost of self-protection
Only costs capable of precise measurement
cards.explanation: The outline is explicit that we consider the cost, including the cost to this defendant, the cost to others similarly situated, and the social costs, if any, of imposing the duty — and adds that this is social policy, not math.
cards.why: Imposing a duty binds an entire class of actors, not just this defendant.

cards.scenario: A plaintiff shows real risk and a precisely quantified, moderate cost of avoidance. Must the court impose a duty?
options: Yes — if cost is less than risk, duty follows arithmetically
Not necessarily — the comparison is not arithmetic but social policy, requiring comparison of incommensurables, and even with measurable risk and cost there might still be no duty
Yes — Hand's formula is a mathematical test
No — cost of avoidance is irrelevant to duty
cards.explanation: The outline stresses that this is not arithmetic; it is social policy, unavoidably comparing incommensurables, and Judge Hand says so himself. Even where there is risk and a reasonably measurable cost of avoidance, there might still be no duty.
cards.why: TRICKY: the B < PL formulation invites arithmetic, which the outline expressly disclaims.

cards.scenario: What does the outline give as the reason for not imposing a duty whose cost of avoidance is too high for the risk?
options: It would violate due process
It is both inefficient and unfair to impose on defendants a cost of avoidance too high for the risk involved
Juries cannot understand such duties
Insurance would not cover it
cards.explanation: The stated rationale is that it is both inefficient and unfair to impose on defendants a cost of avoidance too high for the risk involved. Both halves matter — efficiency and fairness.
cards.why: Fairness is doing independent work here alongside efficiency.

cards.scenario: You are opening the IIED section of an answer. Which issue statement is in the correct form?
options: Whether Δ's constant provocations and actions on the day in question caused π's harm and exacerbated his mental illness, thus providing a claim for IIED against him.
Whether π can establish a prima facie case against Δ for intentional infliction of emotional distress.
Whether Δ was so outrageous that he should have to pay π damages.
Whether the facts of this case add up to IIED.
cards.explanation: The issue asks whether the party can ESTABLISH A PRIMA FACIE CASE for a named cause of action against a named party. It does not recite the facts, and it does not preview the answer. Note also the verb: a claim is established, not 'provided.'
cards.why: Keep the issue at the level of the legal question; the facts belong in the application, and the answer belongs in the conclusion.

cards.scenario: On a trespass to land count, Δ argues π's taunt was consent. Where does that argument belong in the answer?
options: In the issue statement: 'Whether the provocation constituted consent for Δ to enter π's property.'
As an affirmative defense, raised after π's prima facie case is established — consent is pleaded and proved by Δ
In the rule statement for trespass to land
It does not belong anywhere, since consent is never a defense to trespass
cards.explanation: Consent is an affirmative defense, pleaded and proved by Δ. Framing the issue around the defense skips π's prima facie case and inverts the burden. Establish the prima facie case first, then take up the defense.
cards.why: An issue framed around Δ's defense is a structural error, not a wording one.

cards.scenario: Which transition opens an application section in the legal idiom?
options: When looking towards the facts, we can conclude that
On these facts,
This issue is pretty cut and dry, so
I think that based on everything above,
cards.explanation: 'On these facts' — or 'in the instant case' or 'here' — moves straight into analysis. The others are throat-clearing. Option (c) carries a further defect: characterizing an issue as obvious substitutes a verdict for the reasoning that is supposed to earn it. (The idiom is also 'cut and dried,' but the phrase has no place in a legal answer either way.)
cards.why: Never tell the reader how easy the question is; show the work and let the conclusion follow.

cards.scenario: An answer concludes: 'Δ fit every element for a claim of IIED to be brought against him.' What is the defect?
options: Nothing — it states the conclusion efficiently
It asserts the conclusion without taking the elements one at a time and linking the governing rule directly to the facts that satisfy each
It should have said 'fits' rather than 'fit'
IIED has no elements, only factors
cards.explanation: A conclusory sweep across the elements leaves the reader asking which element, and how. Work through them in order — volitional act, intentional or reckless, extreme and outrageous, causation, severe emotional distress — attaching the specific facts that satisfy each.
cards.why: The recurring margin note on unlinked analysis is 'so what?' — state the legal consequence of each fact you invoke.

cards.concept: Exam craft — stating the FI rule
cards.scenario: Which statement of the false imprisonment rule is correctly phrased?
options: …confined to a bounded area which causes harm or awareness and has no means of reasonable escape
…and which causes π to be restricted or confined to a bounded area, with harm or awareness
…locked in a place he could not get out of, causing him distress
…restrained against his will for an unreasonable period
cards.explanation: Absence of a reasonable means of escape is not a separate element bolted onto the end — it is part of what 'confined' means. Stating it twice signals the rule was assembled rather than known.
cards.why: Redundant elements read as padding; the defined term already carries the concept.

cards.text: Trespass to land requires an intrusion {{onto}} real property by a person or tangible substance. In the application, use the past tense: Δ {{entered}} π's property.
cards.why: Small preposition and tense errors accumulate; the professor marks them because they read as imprecision.

cards.prompt: Give the legal idiom for each: (1) bringing a claim successfully; (2) what a defendant does with a defense; (3) what a defendant is when the elements are met; (4) how you introduce your facts.
answer: (1) π ESTABLISHES a prima facie case — not 'provides' or 'has' one.
(2) Δ PLEADS AND PROVES an affirmative defense; the privilege ATTACHES or it does not.
(3) Δ IS SUBJECT TO LIABILITY — not 'is guilty,' which is criminal.
(4) ON THESE FACTS, or IN THE INSTANT CASE, or simply HERE.
cards.fallback: π {{establishes}} a prima facie case; Δ {{pleads}} and proves an affirmative defense; Δ is subject to {{liability}}; introduce facts with 'on these {{facts}}.'
cards.why: Using the right verb signals you know which party carries which burden.

cards.scenario: An answer states: 'This issue is pretty cut and dry. π clearly has a case and Δ has no valid defense worth pursuing.' Two sentences later: 'The only possible argument Δ could have is that his actions did not cause the symptoms. However, we do not have the facts to show that.' What is the defect?
options: Nothing — it acknowledges the counterargument and disposes of it
Two defects: it characterizes the issue as obvious rather than analyzing it, and it raises an argument it concedes cannot be made on these facts
It should have cited a case
It is too short
cards.explanation: Subjective characterizations — 'cut and dry,' 'clearly,' 'no valid defense worth pursuing,' 'there was no question' — assert conclusions the analysis is supposed to establish. Strike them and the reasoning has to stand on its own. Separately, floating an argument you concede the record will not support spends words without advancing anything: if the facts support a causation argument, make it and explain why it fails; if they do not, leave it out.
cards.why: Conclusory adverbs are the tell that analysis is missing underneath.

cards.scenario: Which sentence does analytical work rather than merely asserting a conclusion?
options: Δ clearly committed trespass to land twice, and π obviously has no defense worth pursuing.
Δ entered π's land on two occasions — once to lock the shed and once to unlock it — and each entry interfered with π's right to exclusive possession.
There was no question this was a purposeful act.
This issue is pretty cut and dried.
cards.explanation: Words like 'clearly,' 'obviously,' 'no question,' and 'cut and dried' announce a result without supplying the reasoning. The correct option names the conduct, ties it to the element it satisfies, and states the legal consequence — leaving the reader to draw the obvious conclusion rather than being told it is obvious.
cards.why: If a sentence still works with the adverb deleted, the adverb was doing nothing; if it collapses, the analysis was missing.
